🖥️ Topic 1: Hypervisors — Concepts, Types & Reference Model Very High Priority
5 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 1.1 What is a Hypervisor? & Key Responsibilities
Definition ▼
Exam-Ready Definition: Hypervisor / Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM)
A Hypervisor, also known as a Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM), is a specialized software layer, firmware, or hardware that allows multiple operating systems to run concurrently on a single physical host machine by abstracting physical CPU, memory, storage, and I/O resources.
Main Responsibilities of a Hypervisor (Table from Slides):
ResponsibilityDetailed Explanation
VM CreationInstantiates, boots, and configures new virtual machine instances.
CPU AllocationSchedules and divides physical CPU cores into virtual cores (vCPUs).
Memory AllocationDynamically partitions physical RAM pages among competing guest VMs.
Storage ManagementAllocates virtual disks (vDisks) from physical hard drives or SAN.
Network ManagementProvisions virtual switches (vSwitch) and virtual NICs for guest communication.
Isolation EnforcementStrictly isolates VM memory spaces so one VM cannot peek into another.
VM Execution ControlMonitors instruction flow, state changes, pausing, snapshots, and migration.
Exam Summary: Hypervisor = Executive Manager of Virtual Machines.
▶ 1.2 Type 1 Hypervisor (Bare-Metal) — Architecture, Examples, Pros & Cons
Architecture ▼
Definition: Type 1 Hypervisor
A Type 1 Hypervisor runs directly on the host's physical bare-metal hardware without an intermediate host operating system. It possesses direct hardware control.

Architecture Stack: Physical Hardware → Type 1 Hypervisor → Guest Virtual Machines (OS + Apps).

📸 Visual References Real architecture diagrams & Google Image photos for exam revision:
🔍 Search Google Images ↗ 🌐 Wikimedia Commons Hypervisor Diagram ↗
✏️ 7-Mark Drawing Tip: Type 1 = Hardware -> Hypervisor -> VMs. Type 2 = Hardware -> Host OS -> Hypervisor -> VMs. Emphasize that Type 1 has NO Host OS!
Figure 4.1: Type 1 (Bare-Metal) vs Type 2 (Hosted) Hypervisor Architecture.
Advantages:
  • Maximum Performance: Direct hardware execution without host OS overhead.
  • Robust Security & Isolation: Smaller attack surface; no underlying host OS to hack.
  • High Resource Efficiency: Dedicated strictly to running guest VMs.
Disadvantages & Use Cases:
  • Setup Complexity: Requires dedicated physical server hardware.
  • Specialized Management: Configured via remote management consoles.
  • Industry Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM, Xen.
  • Ideal For: Enterprise cloud datacenters (AWS, Azure, GCP).
▶ 1.3 Type 2 Hypervisor (Hosted) — Architecture, Examples, Pros & Cons
Architecture ▼
Definition: Type 2 Hypervisor
A Type 2 Hypervisor runs as an application process on top of a conventional host operating system (e.g. Windows 11, macOS, Ubuntu Linux).

Architecture Stack: Physical Hardware → Host OS → Type 2 Hypervisor → Guest Virtual Machines.

Advantages:
  • Ease of Installation: Installs like any standard desktop software (.exe / .dmg).
  • Convenient Host Integration: Easily share clipboard, folders, and USB devices.
  • Cost Effective: Runs on ordinary laptops without dedicated servers.
Disadvantages & Examples:
  • Performance Penalty: System calls pass through guest OS → hypervisor → host OS → hardware.
  • Single Point of Host Failure: If host OS crashes, all guest VMs crash instantly.
  • Industry Examples: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion.
  • Ideal For: Software testing, student labs, desktop experimentation.
▶ 1.4 Difference between Type 1 and Type 2 Hypervisors (7-Mark Matrix)
7 Marks ▼
BasisType 1 (Bare-Metal)Type 2 (Hosted)
InstallationDirectly on bare-metal physical hardwareOn top of existing host OS as an application
Host OSNot required; acts as specialized micro-kernelMandatory (Windows, Linux, macOS)
PerformanceNear-native, high throughput, ultra-low latencyLower performance due to dual OS scheduling overhead
SecurityMaximum isolation; minimal attack surfaceVulnerable to flaws in the host OS
Resource AccessDirect hardware device driver controlIndirect; mediated through host OS system calls
ComplexityRequires dedicated enterprise server setupSimple one-click desktop installer
ExamplesVMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, XenOracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation
Memory Trick: Type 1 = Hardware First | Type 2 = OS First.
▶ 1.5 Hypervisor Reference Model (Dispatcher, Allocator, Interpreter)
PPT Pages 9-10 ▼

The Hypervisor Reference Model breaks down the internal instruction-handling mechanisms of a Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM) into 3 vital internal sub-modules:

1. Dispatcher

Acts as the central entry gate of the monitor. Intercepts incoming instructions issued by guest VMs and routes them to the appropriate handler routines (Allocator or Interpreter).

2. Allocator

Decides how system resources (CPU slices, memory pages, I/O bandwidth) are allocated to each requesting virtual machine without starving others.

3. Interpreter

Contains trap-and-emulate routines that safely execute privileged instructions (e.g. CPU control register edits) without compromising host stability.

Memory Formula: Dispatcher = Directs | Allocator = Allocates | Interpreter = Interprets.
📦 Topic 2: Virtual Machines (VMs) & Cloud Virtualization Core Concept
3 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 2.1 Definition & Virtual Hardware Components of a VM
Fundamentals ▼
What is a Virtual Machine?
A Virtual Machine (VM) is a tightly isolated software container that runs its own operating system and applications just as if it were a physical computer.
Virtual Hardware Components (Virtual Box / VM Instance):
  • vCPU (Virtual CPU): Logical execution units mapped to physical processor cores.
  • vRAM (Virtual Memory): Isolated address spaces allocated from host RAM.
  • Virtual Storage (vDisk): Represented as files on host storage (e.g. .vmdk, .vdi, .qcow2).
  • vNIC (Virtual Network Interface): Virtual network adapters with dedicated MAC addresses.
  • Guest OS: The operating system installed and executed inside the virtual machine.
▶ 2.2 System Virtual Machines vs Process Virtual Machines
Taxonomy ▼

A. System Virtual Machine

Provides a complete virtual system platform that supports the execution of a full operating system.

  • Allows physical resources of one host machine to be shared among multiple VMs.
  • Example: An Ubuntu Linux VM running inside VirtualBox or an AWS EC2 instance.

B. Process Virtual Machine

Designed to execute a single application process and masks hardware differences to provide a platform-independent runtime.

  • Exists only for the duration of that single application process.
  • Example: Java Virtual Machine (JVM), .NET Common Language Runtime (CLR).

Cloud Types ▼

Application VirtualizationEncapsulating applications from underlying OS for isolated execution.Docker Containers, App-V

What is a Container?
A Container is a lightweight, isolated user-space environment that packages an application together with its binaries, libraries, and dependencies, running as an isolated process directly on the host operating system kernel.

▶ 3.2 Docker Architecture & 4 Core Building Blocks
Deep Dive ▼

Docker operates on a client-server architecture consisting of the Docker Client (CLI), Docker Daemon (dockerd), and Docker Registries.

1. Dockerfile

A declarative text file containing instructions to construct an image.

FROM python:3.12-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

2. Docker Image

An immutable, read-only template built in stacked layers representing file modifications. Used as the blueprint for containers.

3. Docker Container

A runnable, stateful instance of an image with a thin read-write top layer.

4. Docker Hub

A centralized public/private registry to push, store, and pull container images.

Analogy: Dockerfile = Recipe | Docker Image = Packaged Food | Docker Container = Served Dish | Docker Hub = Supermarket.
▶ 3.3 Essential Docker CLI Commands Cheat Sheet
CLI Syntax ▼
CommandPurpose & Action
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .Builds an image named myapp from Dockerfile in current directory.
docker run -d -p 80:8080 myapp:1.0Runs container in background (-d) mapping host port 80 to container 8080.
docker ps / docker ps -aLists running containers / Lists all containers including stopped.
docker stop <id>Sends SIGTERM signal to gracefully stop a running container.
docker rm <id> / docker rmi <img>Deletes a stopped container / Deletes a local image.
docker pull <image> / pushDownloads an image from Docker Hub / Uploads image to registry.
▶ 3.4 Docker vs Container Distinction (From Slides)
Exam Tip ▼
Key Distinction:
A Container is the isolated environment / box where an application and its runtime execute.
Docker is the platform, tooling ecosystem, and runtime engine used to build, package, run, and manage that container.
☸️ Topic 4: Kubernetes (Container Orchestration) Production Scale
2 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 4.1 What is Kubernetes & Why is it Required?
Overview ▼
Definition: Kubernetes (K8s)
Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration engine that automates the deployment, scaling, load balancing, and management of containerized applications across clustered servers.

Why is K8s required? While Docker easily runs 5 containers on a laptop, an enterprise running 500 microservices across 50 servers needs automated scheduling, self-healing, rolling updates, and internal DNS discovery.

Auto-Scaling

Scales Pod counts dynamically up or down based on observed CPU and memory metrics (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler).

Self-Healing

Restarts crashed containers, replaces failed worker nodes, and terminates unresponsive health-check endpoints.

Rolling Updates

Rolls out new container releases gradually with zero application downtime and instant rollback capabilities.

Rule of Thumb: Docker creates the containers; Kubernetes manages the army of containers.

What is OpenStack?
OpenStack is an open-source cloud operating system that controls large pools of compute, storage, and networking resources throughout a datacenter, managed via a dashboard or RESTful APIs (IaaS platform).

▶ 6.2 Step-by-Step 7-Step VM Creation Flow
Exam Question ▼
  1. Step 1 (Login & Auth): User authenticates on Horizon; credentials validated by Keystone, which returns an Auth Token.
  2. Step 2 (Image Selection): User selects OS; request sent to Glance to fetch the base image location.
  3. Step 3 (Compute Provisioning): Request forwarded to Nova API with hardware flavor (CPU/RAM sizing).
  4. Step 4 (Network Binding): Nova contacts Neutron to allocate virtual interfaces, subnets, and security groups.
  5. Step 5 (Storage Volume Attachment): If persistent storage is needed, Nova triggers Cinder to attach a block volume.
  6. Step 6 (Scheduling to Node): nova-scheduler selects the optimal Compute Node based on available CPU/RAM.
  7. Step 7 (Execution): Local hypervisor (KVM) boots the VM instance, which obtains its IP via DHCP from Neutron.
▶ 6.3 OpenStack Physical Infrastructure Nodes
Hardware ▼

1. Controller Node

Runs control-plane management services: Keystone, Glance, Horizon, Nova API, RabbitMQ message broker, and MariaDB state database.

2. Compute Node

Runs the Hypervisor (KVM), nova-compute daemon, and Open vSwitch networking agents to physically run guest VMs.

3. Storage Node

Contains physical hard drives running Cinder volume drivers (LVM, Ceph) and Swift storage daemons to serve block and object I/O.

▶ 7.1 What is Apache CloudStack & Core Components
Overview ▼
What is Apache CloudStack?
Apache CloudStack is an open-source turnkey Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) software platform that pools computing, network, and storage resources to build public and private clouds.
Core Parts of CloudStack:
  • CloudStack Management Server: Single coordinator orchestrating VM placement, APIs, and Web UI.
  • Database: Central MySQL database storing system state and cloud configuration.
  • Primary Storage: High-performance storage hosting running VM disk volumes (SAN, NFS).
  • Secondary Storage: Capacity storage for ISO boot images, VM templates, and snapshots.
  • System VMs: Virtual routers, console proxies, and secondary storage worker VMs.

💾 Topic 8: Cloud Storage — Block, Object, and File Storage High-Yield (7 Marks)
4 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 8.1 Block Storage (EBS, Managed Disks, Persistent Disk)
Block ▼
What is Block Storage?
Block Storage divides data into fixed-size raw blocks, each possessing a unique address. It behaves exactly like an unformatted physical hard drive attached to a computer.
  • Protocol: Low-level SAN protocols (iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NVMe-oF).
  • Performance: Lowest latency, highest IOPS, supports byte-level in-place edits.
  • Best For: Virtual machine boot volumes, transactional relational databases (Oracle, MySQL).
  • Cloud Services: Amazon EBS, Azure Managed Disks, Google Cloud Persistent Disk.
▶ 8.2 Object Storage (S3, Blob Storage, Cloud Storage)
Object ▼
What is Object Storage?
Object Storage stores unstructured data as standalone objects composed of Data Payload + Custom Metadata + Globally Unique Key, residing in a flat logical namespace called a Bucket.
  • Protocol: RESTful HTTP/HTTPS APIs (GET, PUT, POST, DELETE).
  • Performance: Higher latency, virtually infinite exabyte scalability, 99.999999999% durability.
  • Best For: Media files, video streams, website backups, big data lakes, machine learning training data.
  • Cloud Services: Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage.
▶ 8.3 File Storage (EFS, Azure Files, Filestore)
File ▼
What is File Storage?
File Storage organizes data in a classic hierarchical tree of nested folders and named files, accessible concurrently across multiple systems over a local network.
  • Protocol: Network File System (NFS for Linux) and Server Message Block (SMB for Windows).
  • Performance: Supports concurrent read/write and distributed file locking.
  • Best For: Shared corporate departmental drives, CMS media repositories (WordPress), web server clusters.
  • Cloud Services: Amazon EFS / FSx, Azure Files, Google Cloud Filestore.

5 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 9.1 Software-Defined Networking (SDN) & 3-Layer Architecture
Architecture ▼
What is SDN?
Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is an architectural approach that separates the network control plane (decision-making brain) from the underlying data forwarding plane (physical packet movers).
📸 Visual References Real architecture diagrams & Google Image photos for exam revision:
🔍 Search Google Images ↗ 🌐 Open Networking Foundation SDN Standard ↗
✏️ 7-Mark Drawing Tip: 3 distinct layers: Application Layer on top, Control Layer in the middle (Controller brain), and Infrastructure/Data Layer at bottom (Switches). Connect with Northbound and Southbound (OpenFlow) APIs.
Figure 4.4: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) 3-Layer Architecture.

1. Application Layer

Programs expressing network needs (firewalls, routing topology, QoS) communicating downward via Northbound APIs.

2. Control Layer

The centralized SDN Controller calculating global routing tables and installing flow rules on switches.

3. Infrastructure Layer

Physical/virtual packet-forwarding switches (OpenFlow, Open vSwitch) executing packet delivery.

▶ 9.2 Virtual Private Network (VPN) — Remote Access vs Site-to-Site
Security Tunnel ▼

A VPN establishes an encrypted, secure virtual tunnel across an untrusted public network (like the Internet).

A. Remote Access VPN

Connects an individual user laptop to an enterprise corporate cloud network (e.g. employee working from home accessing private AWS VPC).

B. Site-to-Site VPN

Interconnects two complete static enterprise networks securely (e.g. connecting an on-premises datacenter router to an AWS Virtual Private Gateway).

▶ 9.3 Load Balancing — Layer 4 NLB vs Layer 7 ALB & 5 Core Algorithms
Algorithms ▼

Distributes incoming network traffic across multiple healthy backend servers.

Network Load Balancer (NLB) — Layer 4

Operates at Transport Layer (TCP/UDP). Routes based on IP and port with ultra-high throughput (millions of requests/sec).

Application Load Balancer (ALB) — Layer 7

Operates at Application Layer (HTTP/HTTPS). Inspects URL paths (/api vs /images) and headers for microservice routing.

5 Load Balancing Algorithms:
  • Round Robin: Sequential, circular distribution (Server 1 → Server 2 → Server 3 → Server 1).
  • Weighted Round Robin: Allocates proportionally more requests to higher-capacity servers.
  • Least Connections: Directs traffic to the server currently handling the fewest active client connections.
  • IP Hash: Computes a hash of the client's IP to deterministically bind a client to the same server.
  • Least Response Time: Directs requests to the backend server with the lowest response latency.
▶ 9.4 Content Delivery Network (CDN) — Edge Caching & Cache Hit vs Miss
Edge Caching ▼

A distributed network of geographically dispersed edge servers that caches copies of static assets closer to end users.

Cache Hit

The edge POP already has the requested file cached → returns it instantly to the user without contacting origin.

Cache Miss

Edge server lacks the asset → fetches from origin server, caches a copy locally, and returns asset to user.

🛡️ Topic 1: Cloud Security Issues & The 4 Pillars Fundamental
3 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 1.1 What is Cloud Security & The 4 Key Pillars
Pillars ▼
Exam Definition: Cloud Security
Cloud Security is a broad set of policies, technologies, applications, and controls utilized to protect virtualized IP, data, applications, services, and the associated cloud infrastructure from cyber threats.
The 4 Key Pillars of Cloud Security (From Lecture Slides):

1. Infrastructure Security

Hardening physical datacenter facilities, host hardware, hypervisor kernels, and host operating systems.

2. Data Security

Protecting data across its lifecycle using cryptographic encryption, access control policies, and Data Loss Prevention (DLP).

3. Network Security

Isolating communication channels via Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs), subnets, firewalls, and encrypted VPN connections.

4. Application Security

Securing cloud-native software using secure code pipelines, SAST/DAST testing, and Web Application Firewalls (WAF).

▶ 1.2 Major Cloud Security Issues & 4 Risk Categories
Risks ▼

Your PPT categorizes cloud security risks into four major domains:

Risk CategoryDescription & Manifestation
Infrastructure & Architecture FlawsInsecure default configurations, open database ports, vulnerable hypervisors.
IAM RisksWeak authentication, lack of MFA, excessive privileges granted to users or service accounts.
Operational & Strategic RisksInadequate logging/monitoring, absence of incident response plans, poor patch hygiene.
Compliance, Supply Chain & LegalViolations of data residency laws (GDPR), compromised third-party dependencies.
▶ 1.3 Top 10 Best Practices for Cloud Data Security
Checklist ▼
  1. Enforce mandatory Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) across all console and CLI accounts.
  2. Adhere strictly to the Principle of Least Privilege in IAM permissions.
  3. Enable default encryption for all storage buckets, volumes, and databases.
  4. Block public access to cloud storage buckets (e.g. S3 Block Public Access).
  5. Isolate workloads using virtual private clouds (VPCs) and fine-grained security groups.
  6. Centralize and protect audit trails using AWS CloudTrail or Azure Activity Log.
  7. Automate regular operating system patching and container vulnerability scanning.
  8. Never hardcode static API credentials in code; use assumable IAM roles with temporary STS tokens.
  9. Enforce IMDSv2 on all EC2 instances to mitigate Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.
  10. Conduct continuous automated configuration compliance audits using tools like AWS Config.

▶ 2.1 The CIA Triad in Cloud Computing
Core Security ▼

Figure 5.1: The CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) in Cloud Security.
PillarObjectiveThreatsCloud Defenses
ConfidentialityOnly authorized entities can access dataData leaks, snooping, credential theftAES-256 encryption, strict IAM, MFA
IntegrityData remains accurate, intact & untamperedSQL injection, man-in-the-middle, bit rotSHA-256 hashing, digital signatures, TLS

▶ 2.2 Multi-Tenancy & Data Isolation Risks
Multi-Tenancy ▼
What is Multi-Tenancy?
Multi-Tenancy is an architectural model where multiple customers (tenants) share the same underlying physical cloud infrastructure, while their applications and data remain logically isolated.
Security Challenges & Defenses:
  • Cross-Tenant Data Leakage: Prevented by hypervisor memory isolation and per-tenant database encryption keys.
  • Noisy Neighbor Syndrome: Addressed via CPU/RAM quota limits enforced by hypervisors and cgroups.
  • Side-Channel Attacks: CPU microarchitectural mitigations (Spectre/Meltdown patches).
▶ 2.3 The 3 States of Data Encryption
Encryption ▼

1. Encryption at Rest

Protects static data saved on storage media (disks, databases, S3 buckets, archives). Encrypted via AES-256 with KMS keys.

2. Encryption in Transit

Protects data traveling over public or private networks between client and server. Secured via TLS 1.3, HTTPS, and IPsec VPN.

3. Encryption in Use

Protects active data in CPU cache and RAM during active processing using hardware Confidential Computing (Intel SGX, AMD SEV).

4 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 3.1 Cloud Privacy & Shared Responsibility for Privacy
Privacy ▼
What is Cloud Privacy?
Cloud Privacy focuses on rights and controls governing how personal data (Personally Identifiable Information - PII) is collected, stored, processed, and shared in cloud environments.

Shared Responsibility for Privacy: Cloud providers ensure datacenter physical security and compliance certifications; customers are responsible for data classification, consent management, access restrictions, and privacy policies.

▶ 3.2 Cloud Governance Framework
Governance ▼

The structured framework of rules, roles, and policies to control cloud adoption:

1. Policies

Rules governing allowable cloud resource creation.

2. Cost Control

Enforcing budget limits and tagging discipline.

3. Risk & Audit

Monitoring configuration drift and policy violations.

▶ 3.4 Data Residency vs Data Sovereignty & Cloud Audit
Residency ▼

Data Residency

The geographic location where data is physically stored (e.g. choosing an AWS datacenter region in Mumbai).

Data Sovereignty

The legal doctrine that data is subject to the local laws and subpoena authority of the nation where it physically sits.

🔑 Topic 4: Authentication vs Authorization Core IAM

▶ 4.1 Authentication ("Who are you?") Methods
AuthN ▼
Authentication (AuthN) verifies claimed identity before access is allowed ("Who are you?").
  • Password / PIN: Knowledge factor (something you know).
  • MFA / OTP Tokens: Possession factor (something you have).
  • Biometrics: Inherence factor (something you are — FaceID, Fingerprint).
  • Single Sign-On (SSO): Log in once to authenticate across multiple integrated applications.

🏛️ Topic 5: AWS Identity & Access Management (IAM) Deep Dive High-Yield (10 Marks)
5 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 5.1 Core Concepts: Users, Groups, Roles & Policies (Prof. Amin Shaikh Notes)
IAM Entities ▼

From the official lecture slides by Prof. Amin Shaikh (CSE Dept, GSFC University):

1. IAM Users

Individual persons or service accounts with long-term credentials (password for console, access key ID + secret key for CLI).

2. IAM Groups

Collections of users (e.g. Developers, Admins). Policies attached to the group apply automatically to all members.

3. IAM Roles

Identities with permissions designed to be assumed temporarily by EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or federated users (provides temporary STS credentials).

4. IAM Policies

Declarative JSON documents formally defining permissions (Allow or Deny) on specific resources.

▶ 5.2 Anatomy of an IAM JSON Policy & ARN Format
JSON & ARN ▼ 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:ListBucket"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-gsfc-bucket/*",
      "Condition": {
        "IpAddress": { "aws:SourceIp": "192.168.1.0/24" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Amazon Resource Name (ARN) Anatomy:
arn:partition:service:region:account-id:resource
Example: arn:aws:ec2:ap-south-1:123456789012:instance/i-0123456789abcdef0
▶ 5.3 5 Types of IAM Policies
Policy Types ▼
  1. Identity-Based Policies: Attached directly to Users, Groups, or Roles.
  2. Resource-Based Policies: Attached to AWS resources (e.g. S3 Bucket Policy) for cross-account access.
  3. Permissions Boundaries: Managed policies that set the maximum permissions an identity can receive.
  4. Service Control Policies (SCPs): Organization-level guardrails applied across AWS member accounts.
  5. Session Policies: Temporary policies passed when assuming a role via AWS STS.

Cardinal Rule ▼

Exam Rule to Remember:
All requests start as Implicitly Denied. An Explicit Deny immediately and unconditionally trumps all Allow statements!
▶ 5.5 Principle of Least Privilege & Best Practices
Best Practices ▼

Principle of Least Privilege: Grant users, roles, and applications only the absolute minimum set of permissions necessary to complete their required tasks.

  • Lock away the AWS Root user access keys.
  • Enforce MFA on all accounts.
  • Use IAM Roles instead of hardcoding static credentials.
  • Audit unused credentials with IAM Access Analyzer.

Threats ▼
  • VM Escape: A catastrophic exploit where malware inside a guest VM escapes virtual boundaries to execute code on the host hypervisor.
  • Side-Channel Attacks: Exploiting CPU cache timing (Spectre/Meltdown) to read neighbor VM memory.
  • Unpatched Guest OS: Leaving guest systems vulnerable to network exploits.

📈 Topic 7: Cloud Resource Management — Scalability vs Elasticity High-Yield (7 Marks)
3 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 7.1 Scalability: Vertical (Scale Up), Horizontal (Scale Out), Diagonal
Scalability ▼

Vertical (Scale Up)

Adding more CPU cores or RAM to an existing machine (e.g. 4GB → 16GB RAM). Limited by physical hardware boundaries; requires reboot downtime.

Horizontal (Scale Out)

Adding more server nodes/instances to the computing pool behind a load balancer (e.g. 2 → 6 instances). High fault tolerance.

Diagonal Scaling

Combines vertical and horizontal: scale up individual instances first, then scale out horizontally as traffic expands.

▶ 7.2 Elasticity: Definition & Dynamic Real-Time Adaptation
Elasticity ▼
What is Elasticity?
Elasticity is the ability of cloud computing resources to automatically scale up/out during demand spikes and scale down/in when demand subsides, optimizing costs dynamically.

Example: An online shopping portal runs on 2 servers during regular hours, automatically scales to 10 servers during Black Friday sales, and contracts back to 2 servers afterward.

▶ 7.3 Scalability vs Elasticity Comparison Matrix (7 Marks)
7 Marks ▼
DimensionScalabilityElasticity
DefinitionAbility to handle growing workloads by expanding capacityAbility to dynamically grow and shrink matching real-time demand
DirectionUnidirectional (Scale Up or Out)Bidirectional (Scale Out and Scale In)
AutomationOften manual or planned capacity expansionFully automated in real time via metric triggers
FocusMeeting peak demand without crashingMinimizing cloud cost by avoiding idle resources
🚨 Topic 8: Real-World Cloud Security Incidents (7 Case Studies) High-Yield (10 Marks)
7 Sub-topics ▼
▶ 8.1 Capital One Data Breach (2019) — AWS SSRF & WAF Flaw
AWS ▼

Provider: AWS | Impact: 106 Million customer records exfiltrated.

Vulnerability: A misconfigured Web Application Firewall (ModSecurity WAF) hosted on EC2 was vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).

Exploit: Attacker queried the EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv1) at 169.254.169.254 to extract temporary IAM credentials, using them to download credit card applications from S3.

Lesson: Migrate to IMDSv2, enforce strict IAM least-privilege, and audit WAF rules.

▶ 8.2 AWS Misconfigured Storage Incidents (Public S3 Buckets)
AWS ▼

Vulnerability: System administrators inadvertently configured S3 bucket ACLs to AllUsers (Public Read).

Impact: Automated scrapers harvested millions of sensitive military and medical records.

Lesson: Enable S3 "Block Public Access" at the root account level by default.

▶ 8.3 AWS Customer Credential Attacks (Hardcoded Keys on GitHub)
AWS ▼

Vulnerability: Developers accidentally committed root/IAM access keys into public code repositories.

Impact: Botnets seized accounts to launch GPU compute clusters for cryptocurrency mining.

Lesson: Never hardcode static credentials; use IAM Roles with temporary credentials and secret scanners.

▶ 8.4 Storm-0558 Token Forgery Incident (2023) — Microsoft Cloud
Azure ▼

Provider: Microsoft Azure / Microsoft Cloud | Impact: ~25 government and enterprise email accounts compromised.

Vulnerability: Threat actors acquired an inactive Microsoft consumer signing key (MSA key) leaked via crash dump, exploiting key-validation flaws to forge OpenID tokens.

Lesson: Cryptographic signing keys must be strictly isolated and key validation must not cross trust boundaries.

▶ 8.5 Midnight Blizzard Targeted Activity (2024) — Microsoft Password Spray
Azure ▼

Vulnerability: Password spray attack compromised a legacy, non-production test tenant account that lacked MFA.

Impact: Exploited test OAuth application permissions to view internal corporate emails.

Lesson: Enforce mandatory MFA across all legacy/test accounts and eliminate dormant OAuth apps.

▶ 8.6 Google Cloud Customer Configuration Exposures
GCP ▼

Vulnerability: Misconfigured GCP Cloud Storage bucket IAM bindings with allUsers roles exposed corporate datasets.

Lesson: Security follows the Shared Responsibility Model — customer configuration is 100% the customer's duty.

▶ 8.7 Cloud Supply Chain & Identity Compromises
Supply Chain ▼

Vulnerability: Poisoned third-party packages and compromised CI/CD pipeline tokens inject backdoors into production builds.

Lesson: Enforce Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), pin dependencies, and cryptographically sign container images.

🔥 Unit 4 - Q1 [10 Marks] What is virtualization? Compare its different types in detail. ▼
Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 10 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (10 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Formal definition of Virtualization, Popek-Goldberg Theorem & the x86 virtualization hole.
  • 4 Marks: Detailed explanation of 5 key virtualization types (Full, Para, Hardware-Assisted, OS-Level, Storage/Network).
  • 3 Marks: Side-by-side comparison table evaluating Guest OS modification, performance overhead, and isolation.
  • 1 Mark: Real-world examples (VMware ESXi, Xen, KVM, Docker, Ceph).

1. Formal Definition of Virtualization

Virtualization is the fundamental enabling technology of modern Cloud Computing. It is a software abstraction technique that decouples physical computer hardware (processors, memory chips, disk controllers, and network interfaces) from the operating systems and user applications running on top. By inserting a specialized supervisory software or firmware layer termed the Hypervisor or Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM), physical host resources are partitioned into multiple independent, isolated, and logically complete execution environments known as Virtual Machines (VMs).

2. Theoretical Foundation: Popek-Goldberg Theorem (1974)

Popek and Goldberg defined the formal mathematical condition for a computer CPU architecture to support efficient, direct virtualization:

  • Privileged Instructions: Those that execute without trapping only in supervisor mode (Ring 0) and generate a trap when executed in user mode (Ring 3).
  • Sensitive Instructions: Those that manipulate hardware configurations (control-sensitive) or behave differently depending on the execution mode (behavior-sensitive).
  • The Golden Rule: "An architecture is strictly virtualizable if and only if all sensitive instructions are a subset of privileged instructions:"
    Sensitive Instructions ⊆ Privileged Instructions
  • The x86 Virtualization Hole: The legacy Intel x86 CPU contained 17 sensitive unprivileged instructions (e.g., POPF, PUSHF, SGDT, SIDT, SMSW). When executed in unprivileged mode, they failed silently without trapping to the hypervisor, making pure hardware execution impossible until Intel VT-x was developed.

3. Detailed Breakdown of Virtualization Types

  1. Full Virtualization (Binary Translation):
    • Concept: The hypervisor provides a total simulation of the underlying physical hardware. The guest operating system requires zero modifications and is completely unaware that it is running inside a virtual machine.
    • Mechanism: Non-sensitive instructions execute directly on the bare CPU at native speeds. Sensitive non-privileged instructions are intercepted dynamically and rewritten into safe instruction blocks using Binary Translation in software.
    • Pros & Cons: Total OS compatibility (runs stock Windows/Linux ISOs), but incurs a 5% to 15% CPU translation performance penalty.
    • Examples: Original VMware ESXi, Microsoft Virtual PC, VMware Workstation.
  2. Paravirtualization (Hypercalls):
    • Concept: The guest operating system's source code is intentionally modified to make it "hypervisor-aware".
    • Mechanism: Sensitive instructions in the guest kernel are stripped out and replaced at compile-time with Hypercalls (software interrupts directed to the hypervisor, analogous to system calls from user space to kernel space).
    • Pros & Cons: Near-native execution performance with negligible CPU overhead; however, proprietary closed-source operating systems (e.g., Microsoft Windows) cannot be paravirtualized easily without vendor cooperation.
    • Examples: Xen Project (Dom0 / DomU architecture), original Amazon EC2 PV AMIs, Linux KVM virtio drivers.
  3. Hardware-Assisted Virtualization:
    • Concept: The physical CPU silicon is engineered with native virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x and AMD-V) to eliminate software binary translation.
    • Mechanism: Introduces two orthogonal hardware execution modes: VMX Root Mode (full hardware privileges for the Hypervisor) and VMX Non-Root Mode (for Guest OS and applications). When a guest executes a sensitive instruction, the CPU triggers an automatic hardware VM-Exit, trapping into the hypervisor, which emulates the action and resumes the VM via VM-Entry (VMRESUME). Memory virtualization is handled via hardware Extended Page Tables (EPT).
    • Pros & Cons: Maximum bare-metal performance with zero OS modification required.
    • Examples: Modern KVM, VMware ESXi 7.0+, Microsoft Hyper-V, AWS Nitro System.
  4. Operating System-Level Virtualization (Containerization):
    • Concept: Abstraction occurs at the operating system kernel level rather than the hardware level. Multiple isolated user-space environments (containers) share a single underlying host OS kernel.
    • Mechanism: Enforced by Linux kernel primitives: Namespaces (isolates processes, network interfaces, mount points, IPC, and user IDs) and Control Groups (cgroups) (meters and restricts CPU, RAM, and disk I/O quotas).
    • Pros & Cons: Millisecond boot time, megabyte footprint, 10x higher server density; but lacks kernel diversity (Linux host cannot run a Windows kernel container).
    • Examples: Docker, LXC, Podman, containerd.
  5. Storage Virtualization:
    • Concept: Pooling physical storage capacity from multiple networked storage devices (SAN/NAS arrays, NVMe drives) into a unified, consolidated virtual storage pool managed from a single central console.
    • Examples: Ceph, OpenStack Cinder, Logical Volume Manager (LVM), Storage Area Networks (SAN).
  6. Network Virtualization (Software-Defined Networking):
    • Concept: Decouples virtual network topologies (virtual switches, subnets, routers, firewalls) from the underlying physical switches and cabling.
    • Examples: Open vSwitch (OVS), VMware NSX, OpenStack Neutron, VXLAN overlay encapsulation.

4. Side-by-Side Comparison Matrix of Virtualization Types

Parameter Full Virtualization Paravirtualization Hardware-Assisted OS-Level (Containers)
Virtualization Level Hardware level (Binary translation) Hardware level (Hypercalls) Hardware level (Silicon CPU traps) Operating System Kernel level
Guest OS Modification Zero (100% Unmodified) Required (Kernel modified) Zero (100% Unmodified) Not applicable (Shares Host Kernel)
Performance & Latency Moderate (5–15% CPU overhead) Near-Native (1–3% overhead) Bare-Metal speed (<1% overhead) Maximum Native Speed (0% overhead)
Startup Time Minutes (Full OS boot) Minutes (Full OS boot) Seconds to Minutes Milliseconds to Seconds
Storage Footprint Gigabytes (10–50 GB per VM) Gigabytes (5–20 GB per VM) Gigabytes (10–50 GB per VM) Megabytes (50–500 MB per image)

🔥 Unit 4 - Q2 [7 Marks] Explain the role of Hypervisor. ▼
Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Definition and Popek-Goldberg hypervisor operational model.
  • 3 Marks: Detailed roles of the 3 internal hypervisor modules (Dispatcher, Allocator, Interpreter).
  • 2 Marks: The 4 critical cloud data center responsibilities (Abstraction, Isolation, Resource Scheduling, Live Migration).

1. Definition of Hypervisor

A Hypervisor (also universally termed a Virtual Machine Monitor or VMM) is a specialized low-level supervisory software, firmware, or hardware layer that manages, creates, and executes Virtual Machines. It abstracts physical computer hardware (processors, RAM, storage, network controllers) and presents them to multiple guest operating systems as independent, virtualized hardware devices.

2. The Three Core Functional Modules of a Hypervisor

According to the classical Popek-Goldberg Virtual Machine Monitor model, every hypervisor consists of three core operational modules:

  1. 1. The Dispatcher (The Traffic Controller):
    • Acts as the primary entry point for all trapped CPU instructions originating from guest VMs.
    • Inspects incoming instructions and routes them: if the instruction attempts to reconfigure system hardware, it is dispatched to the Allocator; if it is a sensitive non-privileged instruction requiring emulation, it is dispatched to the Interpreter.
  2. 2. The Allocator (The Resource Scheduler):
    • Responsible for deciding how physical system resources (CPU execution time slices, physical RAM memory page frames, I/O bandwidth) are allocated among competing VMs.
    • Ensures strict resource quotas, prevents one rogue VM from starving others (noisy neighbor syndrome), and invokes memory ballooning drivers to reclaim unused guest RAM.
  3. 3. The Interpreter / Emulator (The Instruction Execution Engine):
    • Contains specialized software emulation routines for every sensitive instruction that cannot be executed directly on bare hardware without violating isolation.
    • Simulates virtual hardware registers, virtual BIOS/UEFI, virtual disk controllers, and virtual network interface cards (vNICs) for each guest OS.

3. Four Critical Roles of Hypervisors in Cloud Computing

  • 1. Hardware Abstraction & Overcommitment: Slices physical hardware into virtual hardware units (vCPUs, vRAM, virtual disks). Enables resource oversubscription (e.g., allocating 64 vCPUs on a 32-core physical server because not all VMs peak simultaneously).
  • 2. Strict Multi-Tenant Security Isolation: Enforces memory boundary protection. A crash, blue-screen, kernel panic, or malware infection inside VM #1 cannot breach or affect VM #2 on the same host.
  • 3. Dynamic Workload Balancing: Constantly monitors host physical utilization and dynamically throttles or expands VM resource allocations in real-time.
  • 4. High Availability & Live Migration (vMotion): Enables migrating an entire running VM—including its live memory state and running TCP connections—from physical Host A to physical Host B with zero downtime for hardware maintenance.

4. Type 1 vs Type 2 Architecture Summary

  • Type 1 (Bare-Metal): Runs directly on raw physical hardware (e.g., VMware ESXi, KVM, Microsoft Hyper-V, Xen). Low latency, high enterprise security.
  • Type 2 (Hosted): Runs as a user application inside an existing Host OS (e.g., Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). Suffers double-OS overhead; ideal for local development.

🔥 Unit 4 - Q3 [7 Marks] Differentiate between Container and docker in detail. ▼
Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Clear conceptual distinction between the runtime unit (Container) and the tooling platform (Docker).
  • 2 Marks: Linux kernel mechanics underlying containers (Namespaces and Control Groups).
  • 2 Marks: Docker architectural components (Dockerfile, Image, Daemon, Containerd, Registry).
  • 1 Mark: Side-by-side comparison table and alternative container technologies (Podman, LXC, CRI-O).

1. The Fundamental Distinction

Students frequently conflate "Container" and "Docker" as interchangeable terms. In reality:

  • Container: An isolated, sandboxed user-space operating environment running as an ordinary process on the host Linux kernel. It is a standardized operating concept governed by the Open Container Initiative (OCI).
  • Docker: A complete, open-source software suite and ecosystem created by Solomon Hykes (Docker, Inc.) in 2013 that automated, simplified, and popularized the creation, deployment, and management of Linux containers.

2. What Makes a Container? (Linux Kernel Primitives)

A container does not have a hypervisor; it is constructed using two native Linux kernel features:

  • Linux Namespaces (Isolation): Partitions system resources so each container sees its own dedicated virtual world:
    • PID (Process IDs — container has its own PID 1 init process).
    • NET (Network — private virtual network interface, IP address, and routing table).
    • MNT (Mount — isolated file system root chroot).
    • IPC (Inter-Process Communication — isolated shared memory).
    • UTS (Hostname & domain name isolation).
    • USER (Maps container root user to an unprivileged user on host).
  • Control Groups / cgroups (Resource Quotas): Restricts, prioritizes, and accounts for resource consumption (e.g., restricting Container A to a maximum of 2 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM).

3. What Does Docker Provide?

Docker wraps raw Linux namespaces and cgroups into a seamless developer developer experience:

  1. Dockerfile: Plaintext configuration script containing declarative build commands (FROM, RUN, COPY, EXPOSE, CMD).
  2. Docker Image: A read-only, multi-layered binary template containing the application code, runtime, system libraries, and settings.
  3. Docker Daemon (dockerd): Persistent background service that manages images, networks, storage volumes, and container lifecycles.
  4. Containerd & runc: Low-level OCI-compliant runtime executing containers on the host.
  5. Docker Hub: Cloud-based public/private registry storing millions of shareable container images.

4. Side-by-Side Comparison: Container vs Docker

ParameterContainerDocker
What It IsThe runtime instance / isolated process executing on OSThe software platform, tooling engine, and ecosystem
Layer of OperationOperating System Kernel (Namespaces & cgroups)User-space CLI, background daemon, build tools & registries
Governance & StandardsOpen Container Initiative (OCI Runtime Spec)Commercial product governed by Docker, Inc. / Moby Project
Image Build SystemConsumes pre-built OCI rootfs imagesBuilds images automatically using docker build & Dockerfiles
DependencyDoes NOT require Docker to run (can run via Podman/CRI-O)Requires a container runtime (containerd/runc) to spawn containers
AlternativesLXC, OpenVZ, FreeBSD Jails, Solaris ZonesPodman, Buildah, Kaniko, Containerd, CRI-O

Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 10 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (10 Marks):
  • 3 Marks: Architectural contrast between Hardware Virtualization (VM) and OS Virtualization (Containers) with diagrams.
  • 4 Marks: Comprehensive comparison table covering at least 8 technical parameters.
  • 2 Marks: Explicit evaluation: Performance Preference vs Convenience Preference.
  • 1 Mark: Real-world cloud architectural synthesis (Containers on VMs / AWS Nitro / Fargate).

1. Architectural Foundations

  • Virtual Machine Architecture (Hardware Virtualization): A physical server runs a Hypervisor (e.g., ESXi, KVM). The Hypervisor emulates virtualized hardware for each VM. Crucially, each VM contains a complete, independent Guest Operating System (including its own kernel, system drivers, package managers, and background daemons) which occupies gigabytes of RAM before any application code executes.
  • Container Architecture (Operating System Virtualization): A physical or virtual server runs a single Host Operating System. A container engine (e.g., Docker, Containerd) coordinates isolated user spaces using Linux kernel namespaces and cgroups. All containers share the single host OS kernel, eliminating guest OS bloat.

2. 8-Parameter Comprehensive Comparison Matrix

Evaluation Parameter Virtual Machine (VM) Container (Docker / OCI)
1. Virtualization Level Hardware level abstraction via Hypervisor Operating System kernel level abstraction
2. Guest OS Requirement Requires a complete, full Guest OS per instance Zero guest OS; shares the single host OS kernel
3. Startup Time Minutes (must perform full BIOS, kernel boot & init) Milliseconds to Seconds (instant process spawn)
4. Storage Footprint Heavy: 5 GB to 50 GB per VM image Lightweight: 20 MB to 500 MB per container image
5. Memory / CPU Overhead High: each VM consumes 1–2 GB RAM for OS alone Negligible: container consumes only what app uses
6. Server Density Low to Moderate: 10 to 50 VMs per physical server Ultra-High: Hundreds to thousands per host
7. Security & Isolation Hardware-Enforced Boundary: High isolation; hypervisor ring boundaries prevent cross-VM exploits. Process-Level Boundary: Lower isolation; if host kernel is compromised, all containers are breached.
8. OS Flexibility Heterogeneous: can run Windows VM on Linux host Homogeneous: Linux containers require Linux host

3. Which One Is Preferred? (Deep Engineering Analysis)

  1. In terms of Performance: → Containers Are Decisively Preferred!
    • CPU & Memory Throughput: Containers execute instructions directly on the physical host CPU without any hypervisor binary translation, VM-Exit/VM-Entry context switching penalty, or shadow page table overhead. Applications achieve true bare-metal performance.
    • Elastic Scaling Speed: Under sudden traffic spikes, an Auto-Scaling Group scaling EC2 VMs takes 3 to 7 minutes to provision, boot, and initialize. A Kubernetes cluster scaling container pods responds in less than 2 seconds.
    • Resource Density: Cloud hosting costs drop by 40% to 60% because idle guest OS memory overhead is eliminated.
  2. In terms of Convenience & Developer Velocity: → Containers Are Decisively Preferred!
    • "It Works on My Machine" Eliminated: A container image packages code, runtime (e.g., Node.js 20), dependencies, system packages, and environment configs into a single immutable artifact. What runs on a developer's MacBook runs identically in AWS production.
    • Microservice Architecture: Containers enable modular microservices where individual APIs are upgraded, tested, and redeployed independently without restarting the entire server.
    • CI/CD Integration: Automated pipelines build, test, and push Docker images to registries in seconds.
  3. Where VMs Remain Strictly Mandatory: → Multi-Tenant Cloud Security!
    • Public cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP) NEVER run untrusted workloads from different paying customers inside separate containers on a shared kernel. A single Linux kernel zero-day vulnerability (privilege escalation or dirty COW) would allow one customer to read another customer's memory. Multi-tenant public IaaS is ALWAYS backed by VMs.

4. Modern Cloud Consensus: "Best of Both Worlds"

Modern enterprise cloud architectures do not choose between them; they combine them: Containers running inside lightweight Virtual Machines (e.g., AWS EKS nodes running on EC2, or AWS Fargate running on Firecracker MicroVMs). This delivers container velocity and density with hardware-level VM isolation.

🎯 University Marking Blueprint (10 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: History, purpose, and modular open-source philosophy of OpenStack.
  • 3 Marks: Architectural communication mechanism (REST APIs, RabbitMQ message queue, SQL database).
  • 2 Marks: Physical deployment topology (Controller, Compute, and Storage Nodes).
  • 3 Marks: Step-by-step VM Provisioning sequence across all core daemons.

1. Overview & Purpose of OpenStack

OpenStack is the world's most widely deployed open-source cloud operating system. Founded in 2010 as a joint project between NASA (Nebula compute platform) and Rackspace (Cloud Files object storage) under the Apache 2.0 license, it enables organizations to transform pools of commodity bare-metal hardware into a private or public Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud.

2. Core Architectural Philosophy

OpenStack is not a monolithic application; it is a collection of independently scalable, loosely coupled microservices designed according to three fundamental architectural principles:

  • 1. Uniform RESTful APIs: Every OpenStack service exposes public and internal HTTP REST endpoints. External tools (CLI, Horizon dashboard, Terraform) communicate with services exclusively via JSON-over-HTTP.
  • 2. Asynchronous Message Bus (AMQP / RabbitMQ): Internal sub-daemons never block waiting for synchronous responses. Instead, they publish remote procedure call (RPC) messages onto a central RabbitMQ messaging queue.
  • 3. Centralized Relational State Database: Persistent cluster metadata, IP allocation tables, VM states, and volume mappings are maintained in an enterprise relational database (typically MariaDB / Galera Cluster).

3. Physical Deployment Node Topology

In a production OpenStack data center, servers are segregated into three distinct functional node roles:

  1. Controller Nodes (The Management Brain): Run the API services, RabbitMQ message broker, MariaDB database, Keystone identity service, Nova scheduling daemons, and network management services. Deployed in high-availability clusters (minimum 3 controllers with Corosync/Pacemaker).
  2. Compute Nodes (The Hypervisor Fleet): Dedicated physical servers running nova-compute, an Open vSwitch / Linux bridge agent, and a bare-metal hypervisor (predominantly KVM managed via libvirt). These nodes execute customer VMs.
  3. Storage Nodes (The Persistence Layer): Dedicated servers hosting physical disk arrays running cinder-volume (Block Storage over iSCSI or Ceph RBD) and swift-storage (Object Storage rings).

4. Step-by-Step VM Provisioning Sequence

  1. Authentication: Tenant sends credentials to Keystone; Keystone validates credentials and returns a scoped authentication token and service catalog URL.
  2. Request Submission: Tenant submits VM launch request (specifying image ID, flavor/vCPU size, and network) to nova-api with the Keystone token.
  3. Token Verification: nova-api verifies token validity with Keystone and writes an initial instance record into the MariaDB database via nova-conductor.
  4. Scheduling: nova-api posts a message to RabbitMQ. The nova-scheduler picks up the request and evaluates filtering rules (RAMFilter, CoreFilter, AvailabilityZoneFilter) followed by weighting algorithms to select the optimal physical Compute Node.
  5. RPC Dispatch: nova-scheduler sends an RPC cast message via RabbitMQ to the nova-compute daemon running on the selected host.
  6. Network Attachment: nova-compute queries Neutron to allocate a virtual NIC, reserve a private IP address, configure DHCP, and establish security group packet filter rules.
  7. Image Retrieval: nova-compute contacts Glance to stream or clone the base operating system disk image (QCOW2 / RAW) into the host's local cache.
  8. Block Storage Mount: If persistent volumes were requested, nova-compute requests Cinder to map the iSCSI/Ceph block volume to the host.
  9. Hypervisor Execution: nova-compute generates the domain XML file and instructs the local KVM hypervisor (via libvirt) to spawn the virtual machine.
  10. State Finalization: nova-compute publishes a state update to RabbitMQ, marking the VM status as ACTIVE in MariaDB. The user connects via SSH or Horizon VNC console.

1. Comprehensive Analysis of the 9 Core OpenStack Services

  1. 1. Nova (Compute Fabric Engine):
    • Purpose: The foundational core of OpenStack responsible for provisioning, scheduling, managing, and terminating virtual machine instances across the datacenter.
    • Key Daemons: nova-api (accepts HTTP REST commands), nova-scheduler (picks optimal compute host based on RAM/CPU weights), nova-conductor (interacts with database on behalf of compute nodes to prevent direct DB access), and nova-compute (interfaces directly with KVM/QEMU via libvirt).
  2. 2. Keystone (Identity & Access Management):
    • Purpose: The universal authentication, authorization, and service discovery backbone. Every single API request across OpenStack must present a valid Keystone-issued token.
    • Key Functions: User authentication, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), multi-tenant project isolation, and managing the Service Catalog (a dynamic directory of API endpoint URLs for all active services).
  3. 3. Neutron (Software-Defined Networking - SDN):
    • Purpose: Provides scalable, on-demand network-as-a-service between devices managed by other OpenStack services.
    • Capabilities: Creation of private virtual networks, subnets, routers, floating public IPs, security group firewalls, VPN-as-a-Service, and Load-Balancer-as-a-Service (LBaaS). Employs Modular Layer 2 (ML2) plugins with Open vSwitch to manage VLAN and VXLAN overlay tunnels.
  4. 4. Glance (Virtual Machine Image Service):
    • Purpose: Discovery, registration, metadata management, and delivery of virtual disk images used as boot templates for VMs.
    • Supported Formats: QCOW2 (QEMU copy-on-write), RAW, VMDK (VMware), VHD, and AMI. Can store backing image data on local filesystem, Ceph RBD, or OpenStack Swift.
  5. 5. Cinder (Persistent Block Storage):
    • Purpose: Provisions and attaches persistent, low-latency block-level storage volumes to running Nova instances.
    • Key Characteristics: Data persists independently of VM lifecycles (unlike ephemeral root disks). Supports live volume snapshotting, cloning, and multi-attach over iSCSI, Fibre Channel, or Ceph.
  6. 6. Swift (Distributed Object Storage):
    • Purpose: Highly scalable, redundant, distributed object storage ring designed to store petabytes of unstructured binary data (videos, images, backups, data lakes).
    • Architecture: Employs a flat namespace without folder hierarchies. Replicates data across multiple physical disks and failure domains, ensuring high durability through eventual consistency over standard HTTP/REST APIs (GET, PUT, DELETE).
  7. 7. Horizon (Web Graphical Dashboard):
    • Purpose: Modern, responsive, Python/Django-based web administration portal for cloud users and system administrators to visually provision resources, view quotas, monitor health, and access VM VNC consoles.
  8. 8. Heat (Cloud Application Orchestration Engine):
    • Purpose: Declarative orchestration engine that automates the deployment of composite multi-tier cloud infrastructure from simple human-readable YAML templates termed Heat Orchestration Templates (HOT).
    • Key Capabilities: Automatically spins up web servers, load balancers, and databases in correct sequence; supports autoscaling based on Ceilometer metric alarms.
  9. 9. Ceilometer (Telemetry, Metering & Monitoring):
    • Purpose: The data collection and metering engine of OpenStack. Constantly polls compute, network, and storage nodes to collect performance counters (CPU utilization, network I/O, disk read/write bytes).
    • Primary Use: Feeds customer usage data to third-party billing engines and triggers Heat autoscaling events via Aodh alarm service.

1. Overview of Apache CloudStack

Apache CloudStack is an open-source, turnkey Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud management platform. Originally developed by startup Cloud.com (acquired by Citrix in 2011 and subsequently donated to the Apache Software Foundation), it is engineered to deploy, orchestrate, and manage highly scalable, multi-tenant compute, storage, and network resource pools in private, public, and hybrid clouds with minimal operational overhead.

2. CloudStack 5-Tier Physical Infrastructure Hierarchy

Unlike OpenStack's decentralized service model, CloudStack structures physical datacenter hardware into a strict, intuitive 5-tier physical hierarchy:

  1. 1. Region: The highest organizational level containing one or more geographically distributed Zones. Regions allow multi-datacenter disaster recovery and global administrative oversight.
  2. 2. Zone (Datacenter): Typically corresponds to a single physical data center facility equipped with redundant power, cooling, and internet network uplinks. A zone contains one or more Pods and secondary storage.
  3. 3. Pod (Rack): Represents a single physical equipment rack within a Zone. All servers inside a Pod share the same Layer-2 switch and Power Distribution Unit (PDU). A Pod contains one or more Clusters.
  4. 4. Cluster (Shared Storage Pool): A logical grouping of identical hypervisor hosts that share a common pool of Primary Storage (e.g., an NFS export or iSCSI SAN). Because storage is shared across the cluster, live VM migration (vMotion) occurs seamlessly between hosts within a cluster.
  5. 5. Host (Physical Hypervisor Node): A single physical server executing a hypervisor (KVM, Citrix XenServer, or VMware ESXi) that runs the virtual machine instances.

3. Comprehensive Comparison: OpenStack vs Apache CloudStack

Evaluation Parameter OpenStack Apache CloudStack
Architectural Design Highly modular, decentralized microservices communicating via message bus (RabbitMQ) Monolithic, turnkey architecture centered around a unified Management Server
Deployment Complexity Very High: Requires complex orchestration tools (Ansible, Puppet, TripleO, Kolla) Low to Moderate: Out-of-the-box turnkey installation; single package deployment
Out-of-the-Box Features Requires configuring dozens of independent configuration files across 9+ services Complete turnkey web UI, billing hooks, firewall, and load balancers pre-integrated
Hypervisor Support Heavy KVM focus; support for VMware/Xen requires complex auxiliary drivers First-class, native multi-hypervisor support (KVM, Citrix XenServer, VMware ESXi)
Community & Ecosystem Massive global ecosystem backed by Red Hat, Canonical, Mirantis, Huawei, NASA Smaller, focused enterprise community governed by Apache Software Foundation
Network Model Extremely flexible, complex SDN abstractions via Neutron (ML2, OVS, OpenFlow) Simpler, pre-defined Basic and Advanced Networking models using Virtual Routers
Best Fit Use Case Large telecom operators (5G NFV), massive enterprises requiring custom cloud APIs Mid-market enterprises and ISPs wanting a reliable, production IaaS running in days

1. Classification of Cloud Storage

Cloud Storage abstracts physical hard drives and solid-state disks into elastic, networked storage resources available on-demand over the network. In modern cloud architecture, storage is categorized along two primary dimensions:

  • Persistence: Ephemeral (temporary host cache that disappears when an instance stops) vs Persistent (data survives VM reboots and terminations).
  • Access Interface & Data Model: Block-level, File-level, and Object-level.

2. The Three Primary Persistent Storage Methods

  1. 1. Block Storage (Raw Disk Volumes):
    • Concept: Storage is carved into fixed-size raw blocks (e.g., 512 bytes or 4 KB sectors), each with a unique physical sector address. It behaves identically to an unformatted physical hard drive or SSD connected via high-speed storage buses (iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NVMe-oF).
    • Characteristics: Ultra-low latency (sub-millisecond), very high IOPS, supports in-place random byte modification, and allows formatting with any custom OS filesystem (ext4, XFS, NTFS).
    • Cloud Examples: AWS Elastic Block Store (EBS), Azure Managed Disks, Google Cloud Persistent Disk, OpenStack Cinder.
    • Ideal Use Cases: Operating system boot disks, high-performance transactional relational databases (MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL).
  2. 2. File Storage (Shared Hierarchical Filesystem):
    • Concept: Stores data as individual files organized in a classic nested hierarchical folder tree conforming to POSIX filesystem semantics. Mounted over standard local network sharing protocols: NFSv4 (Linux) or SMB/CIFS (Windows).
    • Characteristics: Supports concurrent multi-server read/write access with distributed file locking and directory-level permissions.
    • Cloud Examples: AWS Elastic File System (EFS), Azure Files, Google Cloud Filestore.
    • Ideal Use Cases: Shared web application media directories (WordPress wp-content), shared home directories, big data training data shared across computing clusters.
  3. 3. Object Storage (Flat Key-Value Data Store):
    • Concept: Stores unstructured data as complete, self-contained binary objects inside a globally flat namespace (termed "buckets"). An object contains three elements: Data Payload, Custom Metadata, and a globally unique Object Key (URI).
    • Characteristics: No folder tree exists physically. Accessed exclusively over standard HTTP/HTTPS REST APIs (GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD). Delivers massive exabyte scalability, 11-nines (99.999999999%) durability, and lowest cost per gigabyte, but objects are immutable (cannot modify a single byte; updates require full object re-upload).
    • Cloud Examples: AWS Simple Storage Service (S3), Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, OpenStack Swift.
    • Ideal Use Cases: Video/audio streaming assets, static website hosting, automated database backups, artificial intelligence data lakes.

3. Ephemeral / Instance Store Storage

Physical NVMe/SSD drives physically installed directly inside the host hypervisor server chassis. Delivers millions of IOPS with negligible latency. Crucial Warning: Instance store data is ephemeral—if the cloud instance crashes, is stopped, or the underlying hardware fails, all data is permanently lost. Used exclusively for temporary scratch spaces, swap memory, and distributed in-memory caches (Redis/Memcached).

1. Architectural Deep Dive

  • Block Storage (Low-Level Sector Abstraction): Divides storage volumes into raw, sector-addressable blocks. Operates below the operating system filesystem layer. Storage commands are delivered via low-level storage SCSI commands over iSCSI, Fibre Channel, or NVMe-over-Fabrics. It allows arbitrary byte-level modifications at specific byte offsets without rewriting the rest of the disk.
  • File Storage (Hierarchical Abstraction): Exposes a standard hierarchical directory tree with directories, subdirectories, and files. Operates at the OS filesystem layer. Uses network file protocols (NFS/SMB) that handle file locks, metadata updates, and path resolution across multiple clients concurrently.
  • Object Storage (API-Driven Key-Value Abstraction): Eliminates folder hierarchies entirely in favor of a massive flat namespace. Every file is wrapped into an "Object" containing the raw binary payload, extensive custom metadata (key-value pairs describing author, retention dates, tags), and a unique 64-character URI key. Accessible exclusively over standard web protocols (HTTP/HTTPS) using REST verbs.

2. 9-Parameter Cloud Storage Master Comparison Table

Evaluation Parameter Block Storage (AWS EBS) File Storage (AWS EFS) Object Storage (AWS S3)
1. Data Structure Fixed raw addressable blocks (512B / 4KB) Hierarchical directory tree with nested folders Flat namespace (Buckets) with key-value objects
2. Access Protocol iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NVMe-oF NFSv4 (Linux), SMB/CIFS (Windows) HTTP / HTTPS REST APIs (GET, PUT, DELETE)
3. Latency & IOPS Ultra-Low Latency (Sub-millisecond); up to 256,000 IOPS Low to Moderate Latency (1–5 ms); elastic throughput Higher Latency (10–50 ms); high aggregated throughput
4. Concurrent Multi-Server Access Single instance only (Multi-attach rare and requires cluster FS) Thousands of instances concurrently reading and writing Millions of concurrent web clients globally via HTTP
5. Modification Granularity In-Place Byte Modification: Can change a single byte inside a 100 GB database file Append and modify files with file locking Immutable: Cannot alter bytes; updates require whole-object overwrite
6. Storage Scalability Bounded: 1 GB to 64 TB per volume Elastic: Auto-scales from GBs to Petabytes automatically Near-Infinite: Exabytes with zero capacity planning needed
7. Durability Model Replicated within a single Availability Zone (99.999% durability) Replicated across multiple AZs within a region 11-Nines (99.999999999%) durability via multi-AZ Erasure Coding
8. Cost per Gigabyte Highest (~$0.08 to $0.125 / GB / month) Moderate (~$0.30 / GB / month) Lowest (~$0.023 / GB / month down to $0.00099 for Glacier)
9. Cloud Provider Offerings AWS EBS, Azure Managed Disk, GCP Persistent Disk AWS EFS / FSx, Azure Files, GCP Filestore AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, GCP Cloud Storage

🔥 Unit 4 - Q10 [7 Marks] What is SDN? Explain its role in terms of Cloud computing. ▼
Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Formal definition of SDN and core concept of control/data plane decoupling.
  • 3 Marks: The 3-Plane Architecture (Application, Control, Data) and Northbound/Southbound protocols.
  • 2 Marks: Four indispensable roles of SDN in cloud data centers (Multi-tenancy, VXLAN, automation, elasticity).

1. Definition of Software-Defined Networking (SDN)

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is a revolutionary networking paradigm that decouples the network control logic (the Control Plane, which decides where traffic is sent) from the underlying hardware packet forwarding mechanisms (the Data Plane, which physically forwards packets). By centralizing network intelligence in a software-based SDN Controller, network administrators and cloud orchestrators can programmatically configure, manage, and optimize network resources via software code rather than manually configuring thousands of physical switches.

2. The 3-Plane SDN Architecture

SDN organizes network functionality into three vertical logical layers:

  1. 1. Application Plane (Top Layer): Contains cloud network applications and services, including firewalls, Load Balancers, network topology visualizers, security policy orchestrators, and intrusion detection systems. Interacts with the Control Plane via Northbound REST APIs.
  2. 2. Control Plane (Middle Layer - "The Brain"): Houses the centralized SDN Controller (e.g., OpenDaylight, ONOS, OpenStack Neutron server). Maintains a global view of the entire network topology, computes optimal shortest routing paths, enforces QoS policies, and translates high-level application rules into low-level switch forwarding flow tables.
  3. 3. Data / Infrastructure Plane (Bottom Layer - "The Muscles"): Consists of physical hardware switches, routers, and virtual software switches (e.g., Open vSwitch) that have zero routing intelligence. They simply match incoming packet headers against local flow tables and forward, drop, or rewrite packets at line-rate speed. Controlled via Southbound APIs, predominantly the standardized OpenFlow protocol.

3. Crucial Role of SDN in Cloud Computing

  • 1. Multi-Tenant Network Isolation (Virtual Private Cloud - VPC): In cloud data centers, thousands of rival companies share the same physical cables. SDN creates completely isolated logical overlays for each customer, allowing two different customers to use the exact same private IP subnet (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16) without IP collision or cross-tenant packet leakage.
  • 2. Shattering the 4,096 VLAN Limit via VXLAN: Traditional datacenter networks used 802.1Q VLANs, which have a 12-bit ID capping total isolated networks at 4,096. Cloud datacenters house hundreds of thousands of tenants. SDN implements VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) encapsulation with a 24-bit Virtual Network Identifier (VNI), supporting over 16 million distinct isolated networks over standard IP backbones.
  • 3. Instant On-Demand Network Provisioning: In traditional IT, provisioning a new subnet, firewall rule, and load balancer took network engineers days of manual cabling and switch configuration. Under SDN, cloud APIs provision complete virtual enterprise topologies in seconds.
  • 4. Dynamic Traffic Engineering & Auto-Healing: If a physical core switch burns out or a fiber cable is severed, the central SDN controller detects the link failure in milliseconds and instantly reprograms flow tables across remaining switches without dropping existing customer connections.

🔥 Unit 4 - Q11 [7 Marks] Explain the load balancer with one real example. ▼
Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):

  • 2 Marks: Technical comparison between Layer 4 (NLB) and Layer 7 (ALB) load balancing.

1. Definition & Core Purpose of a Load Balancer

A Load Balancer is a physical or virtual reverse-proxy appliance positioned between client web browsers and a backend fleet of application servers. Its primary mission is to evenly distribute incoming network traffic across multiple healthy target compute nodes to maximize system throughput, minimize response latency, eliminate server overload, and ensure continuous high availability with zero single point of failure (SPOF).

2. Core Load Balancing Algorithms

  • Round Robin: Cycles through the server pool sequentially (Server 1 → Server 2 → Server 3 → Server 1). Best when servers have identical hardware specs and requests require equal processing time.
  • Least Connections: Evaluates active TCP connections in real-time and routes the new request to the server currently handling the fewest concurrent connections. Ideal for transactions with varying processing durations (e.g., streaming or database queries).
  • Weighted Round Robin / Ratio: Routes more requests to servers with higher hardware capacity (e.g., an 8-core server receives 4x the requests of a 2-core server).
  • IP Hash: Computes a cryptographic hash of the client's source IP address to consistently route that specific user to the same backend server (useful for maintaining session state).

3. Layer 4 (NLB) vs Layer 7 (ALB) Load Balancing

  • Layer 4 (Transport Layer - Network Load Balancer): Routes packets based strictly on IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports without inspecting packet payloads. Operates at wire-speed with sub-millisecond latency; capable of handling millions of requests per second with static IP support.
  • Layer 7 (Application Layer - Application Load Balancer): Performs deep packet inspection of the HTTP/HTTPS header and payload. Enables intelligent, content-based routing (e.g., routing /api/* requests to high-compute microservices and /images/* to cached storage nodes), terminates SSL/TLS certificates, and manages sticky session cookies.

4. Comprehensive Real-World Example: Amazon / Flipkart "Big Billion Days" Flash Sale

The Challenge: At 12:00 Midnight, an e-commerce platform experiences a sudden 1,000% traffic surge with 500,000 shoppers competing for limited discounted electronics simultaneously.

The Load Balancer Solution Architecture:

  1. DNS Layer (Amazon Route 53): Incoming requests are resolved via latency-based Anycast DNS, directing shoppers to regional Application Load Balancers (ALBs) distributed across three Availability Zones.
  2. SSL/TLS Offloading: The ALB terminates HTTPS encryption using hardware security modules, liberating backend web servers from computationally expensive cryptographic handshakes.
  3. Content-Based Path Routing:
    • Requests to /search and /catalog are routed to an auto-scaled fleet of 200 lightweight web servers backed by Redis caches.
    • High-value transactional requests to /checkout and /payment are routed to a dedicated, high-security target group of memory-optimized compute instances.
  4. Automated Health Checks & Self-Healing: Every 5 seconds, the ALB pings an HTTP health check endpoint (GET /healthz) on all 500 backend servers. If Server #142 runs out of memory and fails to return HTTP 200 within 2 seconds, the ALB immediately de-registers it from the pool. Zero customer transactions fail because the ALB transparently re-routes in-flight requests to healthy instances.
  5. Integration with Auto Scaling: As the ALB monitors increasing request latency, it triggers CloudWatch alarms that dynamically instruct the Auto-Scaling Group to spin up 100 additional instances.

1. The Complete AWS Storage Portfolio

Amazon Web Services (AWS) provides the industry's broadest cloud storage portfolio, categorized into five distinct architectural domains:

2. Core AWS Storage Offerings

  1. 1. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) — Object Storage:
    • Exabyte-scale, highly durable object storage offering 11 Nines (99.999999999%) of data durability by replicating across 3+ Availability Zones.
    • 6 Storage Lifecycle Tiers:
      1. S3 Standard: Frequently accessed data; high throughput and low latency.
      2. S3 Intelligent-Tiering: Automatic cost optimization using machine learning to move objects between frequent and infrequent tiers without retrieval fees.
      3. S3 Standard-IA (Infrequent Access): Cheaper storage for data accessed less frequently but requiring millisecond retrieval.
      4. S3 One Zone-IA: 20% cheaper than Standard-IA; stored in a single AZ (for recreatable data).
      5. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Secure, low-cost archive; retrieval in minutes to hours.
      6. S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Lowest-cost cloud storage ($0.00099/GB/month) for long-term 7–10 year regulatory retention; retrieval in 12–48 hours.
  2. 2. Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) — Block Storage:
    • High-performance, persistent block storage volumes attached directly to Amazon EC2 instances over dedicated NVMe storage links.
    • Volume Types:
      • gp3 (General Purpose SSD): Baseline 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s throughput included free; scale IOPS and throughput independently of volume size.
      • io2 Block Express (Provisioned IOPS SSD): Sub-millisecond latency for mission-critical databases (Oracle, SAP HANA) up to 256,000 IOPS and 99.999% durability.
      • st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) & sc1 (Cold HDD): Low-cost magnetic storage for big data sequential streaming and log analysis.
  3. 3. Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) — Serverless File Storage:
    • Fully managed, serverless, elastic POSIX-compliant NFSv4 file system designed for Linux compute instances and container pods.
    • Grows and shrinks automatically as files are added or removed; concurrently mounted by thousands of EC2 instances and AWS Lambda functions across multiple AZs.
  4. 4. Amazon FSx — Fully Managed Specialized File Systems:
    • FSx for Windows File Server: Native Microsoft Windows SMB file system integrated with Active Directory.
    • FSx for Lustre: Ultra-high-performance parallel file system delivering hundreds of gigabytes per second throughput for High-Performance Computing (HPC), financial modeling, and machine learning training.
    • FSx for NetApp ONTAP & OpenZFS: Enterprise file management with advanced snapshotting and deduplication.
  5. 5. AWS Storage Gateway — Hybrid Cloud Storage:
    • On-premises virtual or hardware appliance bridging local corporate data centers to AWS cloud storage:
      • File Gateway (S3): Local NFS/SMB share backed seamlessly by S3 buckets.
      • Volume Gateway (EBS): Local block storage with automated asynchronous cloud snapshots.
      • Tape Gateway (Glacier): Virtual tape library replacing legacy physical magnetic tape backups.
  6. 6. AWS Snow Family — Physical Offline Data Migration:
    • Ruggedized physical storage devices shipped to customer data centers for offline multi-petabyte data transfers where network bandwidth is insufficient: AWS Snowcone (8 TB), AWS Snowball Edge (80 TB with onboard compute), and AWS Snowmobile (a 45-foot ruggedized shipping container truck transporting up to 100 Petabytes).
