🔥 Unit 4 - Q13 [7 Marks] Explain Kubernetes and compare with Docker. ▼
Unit 4: Virtualization Technologies Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Clear conceptual role differentiation (Containerization vs Orchestration).
  • 2 Marks: Kubernetes architectural components (Control Plane daemons vs Worker Node daemons).
  • 3 Marks: Side-by-side comparison table contrasting Docker (and Docker Swarm) with Kubernetes.

1. Conceptual Roles: Packaging vs Orchestration

A foundational rule of modern cloud engineering: Kubernetes and Docker are not direct competitors; they are complementary technologies that operate at different layers of the cloud stack.

  • Docker (Containerization Engine): Focuses on packaging an application, its runtime, libraries, and configuration into a standardized, self-contained Container Image that runs consistently on a single computer or VM.
  • Kubernetes (Container Orchestration Platform): An open-source system originally designed by Google (Borg project) that automates the deployment, scaling, healing, networking, and lifecycle management of thousands of containerized applications running across a distributed cluster of hundreds of physical servers.

2. Core Architectural Pillars of Kubernetes

A Kubernetes cluster is divided into two primary planes:

  1. Control Plane (The Brain):
    • kube-apiserver: The central REST API gateway and front-end for all cluster communications (CLI kubectl, worker nodes).
    • etcd: Highly available, distributed key-value store that holds the single source of truth for all cluster state, secrets, and configurations.
    • kube-scheduler: Evaluates resource requests (CPU/RAM) and affinity rules to assign unassigned Pods to optimal Worker Nodes.
    • kube-controller-manager: Runs controller loops that reconcile desired state against current state (e.g., if a pod crashes, it spawns a replacement).
  2. Worker Nodes (The Compute Muscle):
    • kubelet: The primary node agent that registers the node with the API server and ensures assigned Pod containers are running healthy.
    • kube-proxy: Maintains network routing rules on each node, handling IP translation and load balancing traffic across Pods.
    • Container Runtime (CRI): The low-level runtime (containerd, CRI-O) that physically downloads images and runs containers.
    • Pod: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes, wrapping one or more tightly coupled containers sharing network and storage.

3. Comprehensive Comparison: Docker vs Kubernetes

Evaluation Parameter Docker (Container Engine) Kubernetes (Orchestration Platform)
Primary Function Creates, builds, and runs individual containers on a single host Automates deployment, scaling, and networking across clusters of servers
Operating Scope Single host machine or single VM Distributed multi-node compute clusters (hundreds of servers)
Basic Operational Unit Container: An isolated application process Pod: Group of one or more co-located containers sharing an IP
Auto-Scaling Manual or basic scaling; requires external custom scripting Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): Scales pods dynamically based on CPU, RAM, or custom Prometheus metrics
Self-Healing & Fault Tolerance Restarts crashed container on same host; if physical host dies, container remains dead Automatic Self-Healing: Detects dead nodes and automatically reschedules pods onto healthy nodes elsewhere in cluster
Load Balancing Basic port publishing (-p 80:80) Built-in internal ClusterIP, NodePort, and external Ingress Controllers
Native Clustering Alternative Docker Swarm (simple, lightweight clustering with limited enterprise features) Enterprise standard with vast CNCF ecosystem (Helm, Istio, Prometheus, ArgoCD)

🎯 University Marking Blueprint (10 Marks):

  • 3 Marks: Amazon ECS (Task Definitions, Services, Cluster architecture).
  • 3 Marks: Amazon EKS (Managed Kubernetes control plane, worker nodes, CNCF compatibility).

1. The AWS Container Ecosystem Architecture

AWS provides an end-to-end container application platform divided into three distinct operational layers: Storage Registry Layer (ECR), Orchestration Management Layer (ECS & EKS), and Underlying Compute Execution Layer (EC2 & Fargate).

2. Detailed Breakdown of the 4 Core Container Services

  1. 1. Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry) — The Image Storehouse:
    • Definition: A fully managed, highly available, secure Docker and OCI-compliant container image registry.
    • Security & Encryption: Container images are encrypted at rest using AWS KMS and transferred over TLS. Access is tightly controlled using standard AWS IAM resource policies.
    • Automated Vulnerability Scanning: Integrates with Clair and Amazon Inspector to scan container images for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) automatically upon image push.
    • Cross-Region Replication: Automatically replicates images across multiple AWS regions worldwide to enable low-latency container pulls for globally distributed deployments.
  2. 2. Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) — AWS-Native Orchestrator:
    • Definition: AWS's proprietary, highly opinionated, fast, and simple container orchestration service designed for deep integration with native AWS services.
    • Core Primitives:
      • Task Definition: A declarative JSON blueprint specifying container images, environment variables, port mappings, CPU/memory shares, and IAM roles.
      • Task: The running instantiation of a Task Definition (equivalent to a Pod in Kubernetes).
      • Service: Maintains a specified number of simultaneous running Tasks, automatically replacing failed tasks and registering them with an Application Load Balancer.
    • Advantages: Zero control plane fee; lightning-fast task scheduling; seamless integration with AWS IAM (granting specific IAM permissions directly to individual tasks via Task Roles), CloudWatch, and Secrets Manager.
  3. 3. Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) — Managed Kubernetes:
    • Definition: A certified, fully managed Kubernetes service that provisions, scales, and operates the upstream open-source Kubernetes control plane across three Availability Zones automatically.
    • Eliminates Kubernetes Maintenance Pain: AWS automatically manages the high-availability kube-apiserver, etcd clusters, automated backups, and version patching with a 99.95% uptime SLA.
    • Pure Standard Compatibility: 100% compliant with standard open-source Kubernetes tooling. Developers use the exact same kubectl commands, Helm charts, and manifest files without modification.
    • Best For: Organizations running multi-cloud hybrid workloads or migrating existing complex Kubernetes configurations from on-premises datacenters.
  4. 4. AWS Fargate — Serverless Compute Engine for Containers:
    • Definition: A serverless compute engine that executes containers on-demand without requiring developers to provision, configure, patch, or scale virtual EC2 servers.
    • How It Works: Works with BOTH ECS and EKS. Instead of choosing an EC2 instance type (e.g., t3.large) and managing OS patching, developers simply define required CPU (e.g., 0.5 vCPU) and RAM (e.g., 1 GB) at the task level. Fargate instantly launches the container inside an isolated Firecracker MicroVM.
    • Security & Billing: Every Fargate task runs inside its own dedicated kernel boundary with zero cross-tenant memory sharing. Billing is calculated strictly on a per-second basis for the exact vCPU and memory consumed while the container runs.

3. Master Comparison Matrix: ECS vs EKS vs Fargate

Evaluation Parameter Amazon ECS Amazon EKS AWS Fargate
Category Container Orchestration (AWS Native) Container Orchestration (Kubernetes) Serverless Compute Execution Engine
Operational Complexity Low: Simple concepts; fast learning curve High: Requires deep Kubernetes expertise Lowest: Zero server management required
Ecosystem & Portability AWS proprietary (cannot run on Google/Azure) Standard CNCF (runs on any cloud / on-prem) Runs seamlessly underneath ECS and EKS
Control Plane Cost $0.00 / month (Completely Free) $0.10 / hour (~$73 / month per cluster) No control plane; pays only for task compute
Server Management Manages EC2 host servers (or delegates to Fargate) Manages EC2 worker nodes (or delegates to Fargate) Zero Servers: AWS provisions microVMs dynamically
Billing Model Pay for underlying EC2 instances Cluster fee ($73/mo) + underlying EC2 instances Pay per vCPU-second and GB-second consumed

🎯 University Marking Blueprint (10 Marks):

  • 5 Marks: Detailed explanation of 7 major data security concerns with specific attack vectors.
  • 2 Marks: Real-world cloud security incident case studies (Capital One, Code Spaces).

1. The Cloud Security Landscape

When organizations migrate to the public cloud, the traditional enterprise security perimeter (physical corporate firewalls, isolated Ethernet cables, and guarded server rooms) dissolves. Cloud data resides on shared physical hardware located in third-party facilities accessed over the public Internet. Under the Shared Responsibility Model, the cloud provider secures the underlying infrastructure ("Security OF the Cloud"), but the customer remains 100% accountable for protecting customer data, identities, permissions, and network access rules ("Security IN the Cloud").

2. Seven Major Cloud Data Security Concerns

  1. 1. Data Breaches & Exfiltration:
    • The Threat: Unauthorized actors gain access to sensitive confidential data, Personally Identifiable Information (PII), or intellectual property stored in cloud databases and object stores.
    • Attack Vector: Exploiting unauthenticated S3 buckets, compromised API credentials, or injection vulnerabilities.
    • Real-World Example: Capital One Breach (2019): An attacker exploited a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) flaw in a misconfigured WAF on AWS to query the Instance Metadata Service (http://169.254.169.254), exfiltrate IAM role credentials, and steal 106 million customer credit card applications.
  2. 2. Data Loss & Permanent Deletion:
    • The Threat: Irreversible loss of enterprise data due to accidental deletion, malicious ransomware encryption, or catastrophic natural disaster destroying datacenter hardware without off-site backups.
    • Real-World Example: Code Spaces (2014): Attackers gained access to the company's AWS root console (which lacked Multi-Factor Authentication), demanded an extortion ransom, and when refused, systematically deleted all EBS volumes, S3 backups, and machine images, forcing the company into immediate liquidation and bankruptcy.
  3. 3. Multi-Tenancy & Co-Location Side-Channel Attacks:
    • The Threat: Multiple competing customers share the same physical CPU sockets, memory buses, and hardware controllers.
    • Attack Vector: Microarchitectural CPU cache side-channel attacks (e.g., Spectre, Meltdown) and VM Escape vulnerabilities, where an attacker breaks out of a guest VM to access the hypervisor memory of neighboring tenant VMs.
  4. 4. Insecure APIs & Management Interfaces:
    • The Threat: Cloud providers expose powerful management APIs that control everything from provisioning servers to modifying network routes. Insecure APIs with weak authentication, broken object-level authorization (BOLA), or lack of rate limiting provide direct remote control to attackers.
  5. 5. Insider Threats & Privilege Abuse:
    • The Threat: Rogue employees, disgruntled system administrators, or cloud service provider datacenter technicians abusing their elevated administrative credentials to snoop on, tamper with, or exfiltrate private customer data.
  6. 6. Cloud Misconfigurations & Overprivileged IAM:
    • The Threat: The #1 cause of cloud data breaches. Cloud systems are complex, and administrators frequently commit disastrous errors: leaving default admin passwords, opening security group ports to the public world (0.0.0.0/0 for SSH port 22 or RDP port 3389), and granting "Action": "*" (Full AdministratorAccess) to service accounts.
  7. 7. Regulatory Non-Compliance & Data Sovereignty:
    • The Threat: Data stored in the cloud is legally subject to the jurisdictional laws and subpoena powers of the physical country where the data center is located. Storing EU citizen data outside European borders violates GDPR and invites fines up to €20 million or 4% of annual global turnover.

3. Defense-in-Depth Mitigation Framework

  • Ubiquitous Encryption: Enforce strong AES-256 encryption for all data at rest via AWS KMS (customer-managed keys) and mandatory TLS 1.3 for all data in transit.
  • Strict Least Privilege & Mandatory MFA: Enforce hardware security key Multi-Factor Authentication for all console access; eliminate root account usage; grant minimal IAM permissions.
  • IMDSv2 Migration: Mandate AWS Instance Metadata Service Version 2 (requiring a session token PUT request) to neutralize SSRF credential exfiltration.
  • Immutable Backups (WORM): Implement S3 Object Lock in Compliance Mode (Write-Once-Read-Many) so neither compromised admin credentials nor ransomware can delete or overwrite backups for a specified retention period.

🔥 Unit 5 - Q2 [7 Marks] Differentiate between Authentication and Authorisation. ▼
Unit 5: Cloud Security & Governance Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Clear conceptual definitions of Authentication and Authorization.
  • 3 Marks: Comprehensive comparison matrix across at least 6 technical parameters.
  • 2 Marks: Concrete cloud architecture workflow (e.g., AWS STS / IAM evaluation flow).

1. Conceptual Definitions

  • Authentication (AuthN — Identity Verification): The security process of validating the claim of identity presented by a principal (a human user, software service, or device). It answers the fundamental question: "Who are you?" It validates identity using one or more factors: something you know (password/PIN), something you have (hardware security key, authenticator app OTP), or something you are (fingerprint, facial biometrics).
  • Authorization (AuthZ — Permission Evaluation): The security process of determining what actions, operations, or resources an already authenticated principal is permitted to access. It answers the fundamental question: "What are you allowed to do?" It is governed by access control policies, access control lists (ACLs), and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) rules.
  • The Golden Rule of Sequence: Authentication ALWAYS strictly precedes Authorization. You cannot evaluate what a user is allowed to do until you have verified with absolute certainty who they are.

2. Comprehensive Comparison Matrix: AuthN vs AuthZ

Evaluation Parameter Authentication (AuthN) Authorization (AuthZ)
1. Core Question Answered "Who are you?" (Identity confirmation) "What are you allowed to do?" (Permission check)
2. Execution Sequence Occurs First (Initial entry gate) Occurs Second (Subsequent to successful AuthN)
3. Validation Mechanism Passwords, MFA OTP, biometrics, digital certificates Access control lists (ACLs), JSON policy documents, RBAC
4. Protocols & Standards SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect (OIDC), Kerberos, LDAP OAuth 2.0, XACML, AWS IAM JSON Policies
5. Modification Frequency Infrequent (User keeps same credentials over months) Dynamic (Permissions change as job duties shift)
6. Visibility to User Visible (User actively types password or scans fingerprint) Invisible (Evaluated silently in the background by API gateway)
7. Failure Result HTTP 401 Unauthorized (Invalid credentials) HTTP 403 Forbidden (Identity verified, but access denied)
8. Real Cloud Example Signing into the AWS Management Console with Username, Password, and a Google Authenticator TOTP token An IAM policy evaluating whether that user is permitted to execute s3:DeleteBucket on a specific S3 bucket

🔥 Unit 5 - Q3 [10 Marks] What is the role of IAM? How does it help to improve security in Cloud Computing? ▼
Unit 5: Cloud Security & Governance Mark Weightage: 10 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (10 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Formal definition of IAM and its role as the new security perimeter in cloud.
  • 3 Marks: Detailed explanation of the 4 core IAM entities (Users, Groups, Roles, Policies).
  • 3 Marks: Six specific technical mechanisms through which IAM dramatically elevates cloud security.
  • 2 Marks: AWS IAM JSON policy structure and the cardinal Explicit Deny Rule.

1. The Role of IAM in Cloud Computing

Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the foundational security framework of policies, processes, and technologies that ensures the right identities (human users, automated applications, and cloud hardware instances) gain access to the appropriate cloud resources for the right reasons at the right time.

In traditional data centers, physical firewalls and network perimeters protected assets. In the modern cloud, Identity is the New Perimeter. Without a robust IAM architecture, every server, database, and storage bucket is exposed to catastrophic compromise.

2. The Four Core Entities of IAM

  1. 1. IAM Users: Persistent identity objects representing individual human people (e.g., a developer or DevOps engineer) or long-term system service accounts. Equipped with long-term authentication credentials: Console Password and API Access Key Pairs (AccessKeyId + SecretAccessKey).
  2. 2. IAM User Groups: Collections of IAM users. Permissions applied to a group (e.g., "DevOps-Admins", "Junior-Developers") are automatically inherited by all members, eliminating the error-prone task of managing permissions individually.
  3. 3. IAM Roles: An assumable identity that does not possess long-term credentials. Instead, any entity that assumes an IAM Role is issued short-lived, automatically expiring security credentials by the AWS Security Token Service (STS). Used by EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or external federated users (via Okta / Microsoft Entra ID).
  4. 4. IAM Policies: Declarative JSON documents that formally define permissions. A policy specifies what Actions are Allowed or Denied on which specific Resources under which explicit Conditions.

3. How IAM Dramatically Improves Cloud Security

  • 1. Enforces the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): IAM allows administrators to grant identities the bare minimum permissions necessary to accomplish their assigned job duties for the minimum required time window, dramatically shrinking the blast radius of any compromised credential.
  • 2. Eliminates Hardcoded Long-Term API Keys: Developers historically hardcoded sensitive AWS access keys inside application source code, which were accidentally leaked onto public GitHub repositories. By attaching IAM Roles to EC2 instances and ECS tasks, the cloud infrastructure automatically rotates and delivers temporary STS session tokens directly into the compute instance memory.
  • 3. Enforces Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): IAM policies can enforce conditional rules that block sensitive actions (e.g., terminating production databases) unless the administrator has authenticated using a physical FIDO2 hardware security key or TOTP authenticator app.
  • 4. Comprehensive Auditability & Forensics: Every single API request evaluated by IAM generates a detailed audit record in AWS CloudTrail (recording the exact caller identity, source IP, timestamp, and API parameters), enabling real-time threat detection via SIEM tools.
  • 5. Context-Aware Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC): IAM allows dynamic policy enforcement based on runtime context conditions (e.g., permitting access only if the client IP originates from the corporate VPN range aws:SourceIp: 198.51.100.0/24, or restricting access between 9:00 AM and 5:00 PM).
  • 6. Absolute Security via the Explicit Deny Rule: In IAM policy evaluation logic, an explicit "Effect": "Deny" statement in ANY applicable policy unconditionally overrides any number of explicit "Allow" statements! This enables enterprise CISO teams to implement impenetrable security guardrails via Service Control Policies (SCPs) that cannot be bypassed by local administrators.

🔥 Unit 5 - Q4 [7 Marks] Differentiate between Scalability and Elasticity. ▼
Unit 5: Cloud Security & Governance Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):

1. Conceptual Definitions

  • Cloud Scalability (Planned Capacity Growth): The inherent architectural ability of a system to accommodate sustained, growing workloads over a medium-to-long-term planning horizon (weeks, months, years) by increasing system resources without degrading performance or re-engineering the application architecture.
    • Vertical Scalability (Scale-Up): Increasing the hardware capacity of an existing node (e.g., upgrading an EC2 instance from 4 vCPUs / 16 GB RAM to 16 vCPUs / 64 GB RAM). Has an upper physical hardware ceiling.
    • Horizontal Scalability (Scale-Out): Adding more nodes of the same capacity to a distributed pool (e.g., adding 10 additional web servers behind a load balancer). Theoretically limitless.
  • Cloud Elasticity (Dynamic Real-Time Adaptation): The ability of a cloud system to automatically, dynamically, and autonomously provision and de-provision computing, memory, and storage resources in real-time response to immediate, unpredictable spikes and drops in workload demand. Resources expand when demand peaks and shrink immediately when traffic subsides.

2. Comprehensive Comparison Matrix: Scalability vs Elasticity

Evaluation Parameter Cloud Scalability Cloud Elasticity
1. Primary Focus Handling sustained, permanent growth over time Handling sudden, fluctuating spikes & valleys in real time
2. Time Horizon Medium to Long-Term (Weeks, months, quarters) Immediate / Real-Time (Seconds, minutes, hours)
3. Trigger Mechanism Strategic capacity planning; manual IT budget approvals Automated metric thresholds (CPU > 75%, queue depth)
4. Scaling Direction Primarily Unidirectional (Growth / Scaling Up/Out) Strictly Bidirectional (Expands OUT and Contracts IN)
5. Automation Level Can be manual, semi-automated, or planned 100% Fully Automated via cloud Auto Scaling daemons
6. Cost Implication Avoids sudden system replacement costs; long-term CapEx/OpEx Direct Cost Optimization: Eliminates paying for idle compute during quiet night hours
7. Target Environments Applicable to traditional on-prem data centers and cloud Unique superpower of Cloud Computing (pay-as-you-go)
8. Real-World Example Upgrading an e-commerce database server instance size to support a business growing 35% annually An e-commerce website automatically scaling from 5 EC2 instances to 100 instances during a 2-hour Flash Sale and terminating them at 2:01 AM

🔥 Unit 5 - Q5 [7 Marks] How can VMs be secured to protect the data and cloud resources? ▼
Unit 5: Cloud Security & Governance Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 1 Mark: Shared Responsibility context for virtual machines in IaaS.
  • 4 Marks: Comprehensive explanation of the 6 core VM hardening layers.
  • 2 Marks: Specific technical configurations (IMDSv2, CIS benchmarks, Security Groups vs NACLs, KMS).

1. The IaaS Security Context

Under the Cloud Shared Responsibility Model for IaaS (e.g., AWS EC2, Azure VMs), the cloud provider guarantees physical host and hypervisor integrity. However, the customer is 100% responsible for securing the guest operating system, application code, firewall ports, user access keys, and storage volumes. Securing virtual machines requires an uncompromising Defense-in-Depth multi-layered strategy:

2. The 6-Layer VM Security Framework

  1. 1. OS Image Hardening (Golden AMIs & CIS Benchmarks):
    • Never launch virtual machines from untrusted public community AMIs. Base all instances on officially hardened CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmark Level 1 or 2 images.
    • Disable all unnecessary operating system daemons, services, and legacy protocols (disable Telnet, FTP, Rexec; allow only SSH key-pair access).
    • Disable root login via SSH (PermitRootLogin no in sshd_config) and enforce passwordless cryptographic Ed25519/RSA SSH key authentication.
  2. 2. Network Microsegmentation & Boundary Firewalls:
    • Private Subnet Isolation: Never deploy database or application VMs in public subnets with public IPv4 addresses. Place them in private subnets accessible only via an Application Load Balancer or Bastion Jump Host.
    • Stateful Security Groups: Enforce strict, minimal ingress firewall rules. Allow inbound traffic only from specific source security groups (e.g., App servers allow port 3306 only from Web tier security group, NEVER from 0.0.0.0/0).
    • Stateless Network ACLs: Implement subnet-level packet filtering rules acting as a secondary line of perimeter defense.
  3. 3. Identity Protection & Mandatory IMDSv2 Enforcement:
    • Use IAM Roles: Never store long-term AWS access keys or database credentials inside VM configuration files or environment variables. Attach an IAM Role to the instance so it receives short-lived STS credentials.
    • Enforce IMDSv2 (Session Token Header): AWS EC2 instances query the Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254. Legacy IMDSv1 was vulnerable to SSRF attacks. Mandate IMDSv2 (requiring a signed X-aws-ec2-metadata-token session token via a PUT request with HTTP hop-limit set to 1) to completely eliminate SSRF credential exfiltration.
  4. 4. Cryptographic Storage & Memory Encryption:
    • EBS Encryption at Rest: Enforce mandatory AES-256 encryption for all attached root boot volumes and secondary data volumes using AWS KMS Customer Managed Keys (CMKs).
    • Confidential Computing: For highly sensitive workloads (healthcare, banking), deploy instances utilizing AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX to encrypt data in flight inside physical CPU cache and RAM against hypervisor inspection.
  5. 5. Automated Patch & Vulnerability Management:
    • Deploy automated patching schedules using AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Patch Manager to ensure zero-day OS kernel security patches are applied automatically without manual SSH interventions.
    • Continuously scan instances for software vulnerabilities and CVE exposures using Amazon Inspector.
  6. 6. Continuous Logging, EDR & Anomaly Detection:
    • Install the unified CloudWatch Agent to ship OS audit logs (/var/log/secure, /var/log/audit/audit.log) to immutable central storage.
    • Activate AWS GuardDuty to analyze VPC Flow Logs and DNS query logs using machine learning to detect compromised instances communicating with known malicious botnet command-and-control servers or mining cryptocurrency.

Unit 5: Cloud Security & Governance Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):
  • 2 Marks: Comprehensive definition and strategic role of Cloud Governance.
  • 2 Marks: The 4 operational pillars of enterprise cloud governance.
  • 2 Marks: Definition of Cloud Compliance and its audit-driven legal nature.
  • 1 Mark: Real-world regulatory standards (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2).

1. What is Cloud Computing Governance?

Cloud Governance is the comprehensive strategic management framework consisting of organizational rules, identity policies, architectural standards, cost controls, and automated guardrails established by corporate leadership. Its goal is to guide how enterprise software teams provision, operate, and monitor cloud resources—ensuring that cloud adoption maximizes business value, accelerates innovation, and controls expenses while mitigating organizational risk.

The Four Pillars of Cloud Governance:

  1. 1. Cost Governance (FinOps): Implementing budget quotas, automated cost anomaly alerts, tagging policies to track departmental spending, and automated shutdown of idle dev environments to eliminate cloud waste.
  2. 2. Identity & Access Governance: Enforcing strict Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), the Principle of Least Privilege, mandatory Multi-Factor Authentication, and automated de-provisioning of employee credentials upon resignation.
  3. 3. Resource & Operational Governance: Standardizing cloud configurations via infrastructure-as-code templates, mandating resource naming conventions, enforcing mandatory metadata tags (e.g., Environment: Production, Owner: Finance), and restricting approved deployment regions.
  4. 4. Security & Policy Governance: Establishing non-negotiable security guardrails via centralized organizational policies (e.g., AWS Organizations Service Control Policies - SCPs) that prevent developers from ever creating public S3 buckets or unencrypted databases.

2. What is Cloud Computing Compliance?

Cloud Compliance is the state of adhering to external legal statutes, industry regulations, government mandates, and contractual security standards governing how sensitive data (PII, financial data, health records) is collected, processed, encrypted, stored, and audited in the cloud.

While governance is internal and self-directed, compliance is external and legally binding. Failure to maintain compliance results in catastrophic legal penalties, loss of operating licenses, and severe regulatory fines.

3. Major Cloud Regulatory Frameworks

  • GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): Strict European Union statute governing personal data privacy. Mandates explicit consent, the "Right to be Forgotten", 72-hour breach notification, and strict data residency rules restricting data transfers outside the EU.
  • HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act): US federal law mandating strict administrative, physical, and technical safeguards (including mandatory encryption at rest and in transit) to protect electronic Protected Health Information (ePHI).
  • PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard): Global information security benchmark required for any enterprise processing, storing, or transmitting credit card numbers. Mandates network isolation, quarterly penetration testing, and zero plain-text storage of CVV codes.
  • SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3 (Service Organization Control): Independent American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) audit reports evaluating cloud service providers against five "Trust Services Criteria": Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy.
  • ISO/IEC 27001 & ISO 27017: International standards specifying best practices for information security management systems (ISMS) specifically tailored for cloud computing environments.

Unit 5: Cloud Security & Governance Mark Weightage: 7 Marks 🔍 View Diagram on Google Images
🎯 University Marking Blueprint (7 Marks):

1. The Golden Cloud Management Triad

Cloud Security, Cloud Governance, and Cloud Compliance are three tightly interconnected yet distinct disciplines that together guarantee the safety, efficiency, and legality of an enterprise cloud estate:

  • Cloud Governance (The Internal Strategy & Rules): The internal policies, budget boundaries, and organizational standards set by executive leadership to control cloud adoption and steer development teams toward business goals.
  • Cloud Security (The Technical Execution & Defense): The hands-on technical architecture, engineering controls, and defensive tools implemented by cybersecurity engineers to protect infrastructure, identities, and data from attacks.
  • Cloud Compliance (The External Legal & Audit Verification): The formal process of proving to external regulators, auditors, and customers that your cloud operations strictly conform to legally mandated standards.

3. The Interdependent Lifecycle

How the Three Work Together in Practice:

1. Governance establishes the internal policy: "All customer credit card numbers must be encrypted and stored only in Frankfurt."
2. Security executes the technical implementation: Engineers configure AES-256 KMS encryption on Frankfurt RDS databases, restrict IAM roles, and block outbound internet egress.
3. Compliance audits the evidence: An independent external auditor reviews AWS CloudTrail logs and KMS key rotation records to certify the company under PCI DSS Level 1.

[2 Marks] Define Cloud Computing according to NIST. ▼

Model Answer:

Cloud Computing (NIST SP 800-145): A model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources (e.g. networks, servers, storage, applications, and services) that can be rapidly provisioned and released with minimal management effort or service provider interaction.

[2 Marks] What is Resource Pooling in Cloud Computing? ▼

Model Answer:

Resource Pooling: The provider's physical and virtual computing resources (CPU, RAM, storage, network bandwidth) are pooled together to serve multiple consumers in a multi-tenant model, dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand without the consumer needing to know the exact physical location of the hardware.

[2 Marks] Define Hypervisor and state its two main categories. ▼

Model Answer:

A Hypervisor (or Virtual Machine Monitor / VMM) is a software or firmware layer that creates, runs, isolates, and manages Virtual Machines on physical host hardware.

  • Type 1 (Bare-Metal): Runs directly on hardware (e.g. VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM).
  • Type 2 (Hosted): Runs on top of an existing host OS (e.g. Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation).
[2 Marks] What is an EC2 Instance and an AMI in AWS? ▼

Model Answer:

  • EC2 Instance: A resizable virtual server running on AWS infrastructure equipped with virtual CPU, memory, network interfaces, and storage.
  • Amazon Machine Image (AMI): A pre-packaged master template containing an operating system (e.g. Ubuntu, Windows Server), application server software, and initial configuration needed to launch an EC2 instance.
[2 Marks] Define Cloud Bursting in a Hybrid Cloud model. ▼

Model Answer:

Cloud Bursting: A hybrid cloud deployment configuration where an application runs normally on private cloud or on-premises infrastructure, but during sudden demand surges that exceed internal compute limits, it dynamically "bursts" excess workloads into a public cloud (like AWS) to maintain availability without crashing.

[2 Marks] What is the CIA Triad in Cloud Data Security? ▼

Model Answer:

The CIA Triad is a fundamental security benchmark consisting of:

  • Confidentiality: Preventing unauthorized access to sensitive data (via AES-256 encryption and IAM).
  • Integrity: Protecting data from unauthorized modification, tampering, or deletion (via SHA-256 hashing and digital signatures).
  • Availability: Ensuring authorized users have uninterrupted access to cloud resources (via multi-AZ redundancy and load balancing).
[2 Marks] What is the Cardinal Rule of AWS IAM Policy Evaluation? ▼

Model Answer:

Rule: An Explicit Deny always overrides any Explicit Allow!

By default, all requests are denied implicitly. If an action is granted by an Allow statement but matches even ONE applicable policy containing an "Effect": "Deny", access is unconditionally refused.

[5 Marks] Explain the 10 Evaluation Criteria for Selecting a Cloud Service Provider (CSP). ▼

Model Answer:

According to lecture slides, CSP selection is governed by the principle: Sustenance = Technology Strength + Business Skills.

  1. Certifications & Standards: Adherence to ISO 27001, SOC 2, Open Cloud Consortium (OCC), and IEEE standards.
  2. Financial Health: Long-term fiscal stability and capitalization of the provider.
  3. Business & Technology Strength: Technical capability and agility to satisfy enterprise requirements.
  4. Compliance Audits: Independent third-party audit validation.
  5. Service Level Agreements (SLAs): Contractual availability guarantees (e.g. 99.99%) and financial credit terms.
  6. Reporting & Tracking: Real-time operational monitoring and immutable audit logging.
  7. Transparent Costing & Billing: Granular pay-as-you-go billing with real-time budget alarms.
  8. Maintenance & Upgrades: Low-friction software upgrades and painless data migrations.
  9. Technical Support: Tiered 24x7 support with guaranteed response times.
  10. Security Architecture: Defense-in-depth, data encryption at rest and in transit, and physical datacenter controls.
[5 Marks] Explain Fog Computing and its industrial IoT applications. ▼

Model Answer:

Fog Computing: A decentralized computing paradigm that extends cloud computing and storage to the edge of the network. Intermediate "Fog Nodes" (gateways, routers, local edge servers) perform real-time data filtering, processing, and analysis close to IoT devices instead of transmitting raw telemetry to a distant cloud.

Key Industrial Applications:

  • Manufacturing Factory Lines: Real-time robotic arm monitoring to prevent machine collision without network round-trip latency.
  • Oil & Gas Pipelines: Local acoustic sensor analysis to detect sudden pressure drops and trigger emergency shutoff valves.
  • On-Flight Avionics: Real-time engine telemetry analysis while aircraft is in flight with limited satellite bandwidth.
  • Smart Traffic & Autonomous Vehicles: Sub-second collision avoidance decisions executed at local traffic intersection nodes.
[5 Marks] Explain the Hypervisor Reference Model (Dispatcher, Allocator, Interpreter). ▼

Model Answer:

The Hypervisor Reference Model (from lecture slides 9–10) decomposes a Virtual Machine Monitor into three core internal modules:

  1. Dispatcher: Serves as the primary entry point of the VMM. It traps all instructions issued by guest virtual machines, inspects their privilege level, and reroutes non-privileged calls or passes privileged instructions to the Allocator or Interpreter.
  2. Allocator: Decides and administers physical resource distribution. Whenever a VM requests additional RAM, vCPU cycles, or storage blocks, the Allocator applies scheduling algorithms to allocate system hardware safely without resource starvation.
  3. Interpreter: Contains specific trap routines that simulate privileged machine instructions executed by the guest OS (such as modifying hardware control registers or page tables), executing them in a protected context without compromising the host.
[5 Marks] Differentiate High Availability (HA) and Fault Tolerance (FT) with the Availability Formula. ▼

Model Answer:

  • High Availability (HA): Ensures a cloud system remains operational with minimal perceptible downtime through automated failover clusters, load balancers, and multi-AZ setups.
  • Fault Tolerance (FT): Ensures zero downtime and zero data loss during component failures through 100% hot hardware mirroring.

Mathematical Availability Formula:

$$\text{{Availability (\%)}} = \frac{{\text{{Uptime}}}}{{\text{{Uptime}} + \text{{Downtime}}}} \times 100$$

Example: 999 hours uptime with 1 hour downtime = $\frac{{999}}{{1000}} \times 100 = 99.9\%$ (Three Nines).

[5 Marks] Compare Google App Engine and AWS Elastic Beanstalk (Web vs Worker Tiers). ▼

Model Answer:

  • Google App Engine (GAE): Pure serverless PaaS with 3 layers (Application, Platform, Infrastructure). Automatically scales down to zero instances; provides zero direct server access.
  • AWS Elastic Beanstalk: Managed orchestration PaaS that deploys underlying EC2 instances while retaining root access for developers. Offers two environment tiers:
    • Web Server Environment: Provisions an Application Load Balancer and Auto-Scaling EC2 web nodes to handle HTTP/HTTPS user requests.
    • Worker Environment: Processes compute-heavy background tasks by pulling jobs from an Amazon SQS queue.

[7 Marks] Compare Block, Object, and File Storage with features, use cases, and AWS examples. ▼

Model Answer:

  1. Block Storage (e.g. AWS EBS):
    • Mechanism: Data split into fixed addressable blocks mounted over SAN/iSCSI.
    • Features: Ultra-low latency, high IOPS, support for in-place byte updates.
    • Use Cases: Virtual machine boot drives, relational transactional databases (MySQL, Oracle).
  2. Object Storage (e.g. AWS S3):
    • Mechanism: Data stored as flat objects (Payload + Metadata + Unique Key) in buckets over HTTP/REST APIs.
    • Features: 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability, massive exabyte scale, cheap archiving tiers.
    • Use Cases: Video streaming, static website hosting, backup and disaster recovery.
  3. File Storage (e.g. AWS EFS):
    • Mechanism: Classic hierarchical tree of directories and files mounted via NFSv4/SMB.
    • Features: Concurrent multi-server read/write with distributed file locking.
    • Use Cases: Shared corporate folders, CMS document roots (WordPress), shared dev repositories.

[7 Marks] Explain Multi-Server 3-Tier Web Architecture and Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing. ▼

Model Answer:

A Multi-Server 3-Tier Architecture decouples an application into three independent layers:

  • Tier 1: Web Tier (Presentation): Reverse proxy and web servers (Nginx/Apache) behind a Load Balancer terminating SSL and serving static assets.
  • Tier 2: Application Tier (Business Logic): Auto-scaling worker cluster processing business logic and REST APIs, paired with an in-memory Redis cache.
  • Tier 3: Database Tier (Persistence): Primary Master database (Writes) replicating asynchronously to Read-Replicas (Reads) across multiple AZs.

Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing:

  • Layer 4 (Transport / NLB): Routes traffic based on IP address and TCP/UDP port without inspecting application packet content. Ultra-fast, sub-millisecond latency.
  • Layer 7 (Application / ALB): Routes traffic based on application payload (HTTP URLs, headers, hostnames, cookies). Performs smart content-based routing (e.g. /api → App servers, /images → S3).
[10 Marks] 1. Comprehensive Analysis of Virtualization: Full Virtualization vs Paravirtualization vs Hardware-Assisted, Popek-Goldberg Theorem, CPU Rings & Root/Non-Root Modes, and 3 Virtualization Domains (Compute, Storage, Network). ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 2 Marks: Formal Definition of Virtualization & Popek-Goldberg Virtualization Theorem ($Sensitive \subseteq Privileged$).
  • 3 Marks: Architectural comparison & diagrams of Full Virtualization, Paravirtualization, and Hardware-Assisted Virtualization.
  • 2 Marks: CPU Ring Privilege structure, Intel VT-x / AMD-V VMX Root & Non-Root execution, VM-Exit & VM-Entry cycles.
  • 2 Marks: Detailed breakdown of Compute, Storage, and Network Virtualization techniques in cloud datacenters.
  • 1 Mark: 8-Parameter comparison table (VMs vs Docker Containers vs Bare-Metal).

1. Formal Definition & Foundation of Virtualization

Virtualization is the foundational enabling technology of Cloud Computing. It is a software abstraction layer that decouples physical hardware (CPU, physical RAM, storage controllers, network interface cards) from the operating systems and user applications running on top. It creates logical, isolated execution environments called Virtual Machines (VMs), governed by a specialized supervisory kernel termed the Hypervisor or Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM).

2. Popek-Goldberg Virtualization Theorem (1974)

Formulated by Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, this theorem establishes the formal mathematical criteria for a computer processor architecture to support efficient, direct-execution virtualization:

  • Privileged Instructions: Instructions that trap (generate a hardware exception) when executed in user mode (Ring 3), transferring control immediately to supervisor mode (Ring 0).
  • Sensitive Instructions: Instructions that inspect hardware configurations without trapping (behavior-sensitive) or modify hardware configurations / memory mappings (control-sensitive).
  • The Golden Theorem: "A computer architecture is strictly virtualizable if and only if all sensitive instructions are a subset of privileged instructions." $$ ext{Sensitive Instructions} \subseteq ext{Privileged Instructions}$$
  • The Classical x86 Virtualization Hole: The original x86 architecture contained 17 sensitive instructions (such as POPF, PUSHF, SGDT, SIDT, SLDT, SMSW) that were NOT privileged! When executed in unprivileged user mode, they simply failed silently or leaked physical hardware register values without trapping. This made standard x86 non-virtualizable without complex software binary rewriting until Intel VT-x hardware assist was released in 2005.

3. Three CPU Virtualization Techniques (Architectural Breakdown)

TechniqueGuest OS RequirementMechanismPerformance & LatencyPrimary Examples
1. Full Virtualization (Binary Translation) 100% Unmodified Guest OS (Standard ISO images) Hypervisor uses dynamic Binary Translation to intercept non-faulting sensitive instructions in software, translating them into safe instruction sequences while user code runs natively. Moderate; carries 5% to 15% translation CPU overhead. VMware ESXi, original VMware Workstation, Microsoft Virtual PC.
2. Paravirtualization (Hypercalls) Modified Guest OS Kernel required Guest OS kernel source code is modified to be hypervisor-aware. Sensitive CPU instructions are replaced at compile time with Hypercalls (software interrupts to hypervisor, similar to syscalls). Near-native hardware speed; minimal software translation overhead. Xen Project (Dom0 / DomU), KVM (virtio drivers), Amazon EC2 original PV AMI instances.
3. Hardware-Assisted Virtualization 100% Unmodified Guest OS CPU hardware silicon provides dedicated virtualization rings (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) enabling hardware-enforced traps via VM-Exit and VM-Entry cycles. Maximum bare-metal performance; near zero CPU virtualization penalty. KVM with Intel VT-x, VMware ESXi 7+, Hyper-V, AWS Nitro System.

4. CPU Privilege Rings & Intel VT-x VMX Modes

Classical x86 utilizes 4 hierarchical rings: Ring 0 (Kernel/Supervisor), Ring 1 & 2 (Device Drivers), and Ring 3 (User Applications). In traditional OS architecture, the OS kernel occupies Ring 0.

The "Ring 0 Contention" Problem: Both the Hypervisor and the Guest OS believe they belong in Ring 0. Running the Guest OS in Ring 1 or 2 breaks device driver expectations.

Intel VT-x & AMD-V Hardware Solution: Intel introduced two distinct hardware execution modes that operate orthogonally across all 4 rings:

  • VMX Root Operation: The hypervisor executes here with full, unrestricted access to physical hardware registers and memory management units. Contains full Rings 0 to 3.
  • VMX Non-Root Operation: The Guest OS and its applications execute here. When the Guest OS in Ring 0 executes any sensitive privileged instruction, the CPU triggers an automatic hardware VM-Exit, instantly pausing the guest VM and passing execution state to the hypervisor in Root Mode.
  • VM-Exit & VM-Entry Lifecycle: The hypervisor inspects the VMCS (Virtual Machine Control Structure), handles the I/O or privileged operation, and executes VMRESUME to perform a VM-Entry, restoring guest VM execution.
  • Memory Virtualization (EPT / NPT): Intel Extended Page Tables (EPT) and AMD Nested Page Tables (NPT) maintain two-dimensional page tables: Guest Virtual → Guest Physical → Host Physical memory, completely handled in CPU silicon.

5. The Three Virtualization Domains in Cloud Computing

  1. Compute Virtualization: Abstraction of CPU and memory. A single physical multi-core socket (e.g. 64 cores) is scheduled into hundreds of virtual CPUs (vCPUs) by the hypervisor credit or CFS scheduler. Features dynamic ballooning and RAM overcommitment.
  2. Storage Virtualization: Pooling multiple physical hard disk drives and flash SSDs from Storage Area Networks (SAN) and Network Attached Storage (NAS) into elastic virtual storage pools. Supported by Logical Volume Management (LVM) and Software-Defined Storage (Ceph, OpenStack Cinder/Swift).
  3. Network Virtualization: Decouples physical cables, top-of-rack switches, and routers into software abstractions. Uses Virtual Network Interface Cards (vNICs), virtual software switches (Open vSwitch), and overlay encapsulation protocols (VXLAN, NVGRE) to create isolated multi-tenant overlay networks.

6. Virtual Machines vs Docker Containers vs Bare-Metal Comparison

ParameterBare-Metal ServerVirtual Machine (Hypervisor)Docker Container (OS-Level)
Virtualization LevelNone (Physical Hardware)Hardware-level (CPU, RAM, NIC emulated)OS Kernel-level (Namespaces & cgroups)
Operating SystemSingle dedicated Host OSFull Guest OS per VM (GBs in size)Shares Host OS kernel (MBs in size)
Startup Boot TimeSeveral minutes (POST & BIOS)1 to 3 minutes (Full OS kernel boot)Milliseconds to seconds (Process spawn)
Resource Overhead0% (Native execution)High (Each VM reserves dedicated RAM/OS)Minimal (Zero Guest OS RAM tax)
Security IsolationPhysical hardware isolationStrong hardware hypervisor boundariesProcess-level isolation (Shared kernel risk)
Server Density1 workload per server10 to 30 VMs per host200 to 500 containers per host
PortabilityLocked to physical hardware driversHigh (Hypervisor image formats: OVF, QCOW2)Extreme (Runs identically across any Linux host)

[10 Marks] 2. OpenStack Cloud Operating System: Detailed Architecture, All 9 Core Components (Nova, Keystone, Neutron, Glance, Cinder, Swift, Horizon, Heat, Ceilometer), Message Queue Communication, and 12-Step VM Provisioning Workflow. ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 2 Marks: Definition, OpenStack philosophy, and architectural communication bus (RabbitMQ & MariaDB/MySQL).
  • 4 Marks: Comprehensive description of all 9 core services with internal daemons and responsibilities.
  • 3 Marks: End-to-end 12-step VM launch sequence diagram and workflow description.
  • 1 Mark: OpenStack High Availability (HA) deployment architecture (Controller vs Compute vs Storage nodes).

1. OpenStack Overview & Modular Philosophy

OpenStack is the world's most widely deployed open-source cloud operating system. It orchestrates large pools of compute, storage, and networking resources throughout datacenters via a set of interrelated microservices. All services communicate asynchronously via the RabbitMQ AMQP Message Queue and store relational state in a shared MariaDB/MySQL cluster. External clients interact exclusively via uniform RESTful APIs.

2. The 9 Core OpenStack Services (Detailed Deep-Dive)

  1. Keystone (Identity & Authentication Service):
    • Responsibilities: Central security authority. Provides user authentication, token issuance (UUID and Fernet tokens), RBAC role evaluation, and a dynamic Service Catalog containing API endpoints for all cloud services.
    • Core Concepts: Users, Tenants/Projects, Roles, Domains, Endpoints (Public, Admin, Internal).
  2. Nova (Compute Fabric Orchestrator):
    • Responsibilities: Provisions and manages the lifecycle of virtual machine instances.
    • Internal Daemons: nova-api (receives REST requests), nova-scheduler (evaluates filter algorithms like RAMFilter, CoreFilter to pick optimal host), nova-conductor (database proxy isolating compute nodes), nova-compute (runs on hypervisor node controlling KVM via libvirt).
  3. Neutron (Software-Defined Networking - SDN):
    • Responsibilities: Delivers Networking-as-a-Service (NaaS), managing virtual networks, subnets, routers, floating IPs, security groups, and VPN/LBaaS plugins.
    • Internal Architecture: ML2 (Modular Layer 2) plugin coordinating Open vSwitch (OVS) or Linux Bridge drivers, L3 Agent (NAT/routing), and DHCP Agent.
  4. Glance (Virtual Machine Image Registry):
    • Responsibilities: Discovers, registers, stores, and retrieves virtual machine disk images and VM snapshots.
    • Supported Formats: QCOW2, RAW, VMDK, VHD, ISO, AMI. Backed by Swift, Ceph, or standard local filesystem storage.
  5. Cinder (Persistent Block Storage Service):
    • Responsibilities: Provisions persistent, raw block volumes attached to Nova compute instances over iSCSI, Fibre Channel, or Ceph RBD. Survives VM termination.
    • Internal Daemons: cinder-api, cinder-scheduler, cinder-volume.
  6. Swift (Distributed Object Storage):
    • Responsibilities: Exabyte-scale, highly durable multi-tenant object storage for unstructured media and backups accessed via HTTP/REST (GET, PUT, DELETE).
    • Architecture: Masterless Ring architecture dividing data into Account, Container, and Object servers with automated data auditing and replication.
  7. Horizon (Web Graphical Dashboard):
    • Responsibilities: Django-based web application providing self-service user management and administrative control over all OpenStack resources.
  8. Heat (Orchestration Engine):
    • Responsibilities: Template-driven cloud application deployment based on Heat Orchestration Templates (HOT) written in declarative YAML. Functionally equivalent to AWS CloudFormation.
  9. Ceilometer (Telemetry, Metering & Alarming):
    • Responsibilities: Collects performance metrics, resource consumption event logs, and billing meters across compute, disk, and network interfaces. Integrates with Aodh (alarm service) for automated horizontal scaling triggers.

3. End-to-End 12-Step VM Provisioning Lifecycle (Sequence Workflow)

Step-by-Step Execution Trace:

  1. Step 1 (Authentication): User submits credentials via Horizon Web UI / OpenStack CLI. Keystone authenticates credentials and issues an unscoped token, then swaps for a tenant-scoped token and the service catalog.
  2. Step 2 (Boot Request): User issues openstack server create --image Ubuntu --flavor m1.small web-vm. Horizon sends an HTTP POST request to nova-api with the Keystone auth token.
  3. Step 3 (Token Validation): nova-api validates the token and project quotas with Keystone.
  4. Step 4 (Database Update): nova-api writes initial VM instance state (BUILDING) into the MariaDB database via nova-conductor.
  5. Step 5 (Scheduler Dispatch): nova-api publishes a message to the RabbitMQ scheduler exchange requesting host placement.
  6. Step 6 (Filtering & Weighting): nova-scheduler runs filtering algorithms (RAMFilter, AvailabilityZoneFilter, DiskFilter) followed by weighting algorithms to select the optimal physical compute host (e.g. compute-node-04).
  7. Step 7 (RPC to Compute): nova-scheduler sends an AMQP message through RabbitMQ to the target host's nova-compute daemon.
  8. Step 8 (Network Allocation): nova-compute contacts Neutron via REST API to allocate a virtual network port, IP address, and security group firewall rules.
  9. Step 9 (Image Fetching): nova-compute contacts Glance using image ID to stream the base QCOW2 operating system image to the local compute node cache.
  10. Step 10 (Volume Attachment): If persistent storage was requested, nova-compute invokes Cinder to map and attach the block volume over iSCSI.
  11. Step 11 (Hypervisor Spawning): nova-compute generates a libvirt XML domain definition and instructs the hypervisor (KVM) to instantiate and boot the VM.
  12. Step 12 (Active State Notification): nova-compute confirms successful boot, updates instance status to ACTIVE in MariaDB, and notifies Ceilometer to begin telemetry tracking.

4. OpenStack High Availability (HA) Production Architecture

Production OpenStack datacenters segregate machines into three functional physical tiers:

  • Controller Nodes (3 Nodes Minimum Cluster): Runs all API daemons, Keystone, Horizon, RabbitMQ (mirrored queues), and MariaDB Galera multi-master cluster managed by Pacemaker/Corosync with HAProxy for VIP load balancing.
  • Compute Nodes (Horizontally Scalable): Dedicated bare-metal servers executing nova-compute, Open vSwitch, and KVM hypervisors. Zero administrative database credentials.
  • Storage Nodes: Dedicated servers hosting Ceph OSDs, Cinder volume drivers, or Swift object storage rings.
[10 Marks] 3. Multi-Tenant Cloud Architecture: Comprehensive Analysis of Silo, Bridge, and Pool Isolation Models, Row-Level Security (RLS) Implementation, Noisy Neighbor Problem, and Mitigation Algorithms. ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 2 Marks: Definition of Multi-Tenancy, economic business rationale, and comparison with Multi-Instance architecture.
  • 3 Marks: Detailed explanation and diagrams of Silo, Bridge, and Pool data isolation patterns.
  • 2 Marks: Concrete Row-Level Security (RLS) SQL implementation and tenant context injection.
  • 2 Marks: Noisy Neighbor problem causes and engineering mitigation algorithms (Token Bucket, Cgroups, Tenant Tiering).
  • 1 Mark: 7-parameter comparison table across isolation models.

1. Multi-Tenancy Definition & Economic Foundations

Multi-Tenant Architecture is a software architecture where a single physical or logical instance of an application runs on cloud infrastructure to serve multiple independent customer organizations, called tenants. Each tenant has a customized, isolated virtual partition with its own user accounts, access permissions, branding, and sensitive data.

Economic Driver: In traditional single-tenant hosting, serving 1,000 customers requires running 1,000 distinct VM clusters, OS licenses, and database instances. Multi-tenancy aggregates workloads onto shared infrastructure, reducing Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) by 70% to 90% and simplifying software upgrades to a single centralized deployment.

2. The Three Database Isolation Patterns

A. Silo Pattern (Dedicated Database per Tenant)
  • Architecture: Every tenant receives a completely independent, physically or logically isolated database instance (e.g. separate AWS RDS instances).
  • Advantages: Maximum data isolation, zero risk of cross-tenant data leakage, customized database configurations per tenant, zero cross-tenant blast radius, simplified tenant-specific point-in-time backups.
  • Disadvantages: Highest operational cost, extreme management overhead (running database migrations across thousands of instances), severe resource underutilization during off-peak hours.
  • Target Domain: Commercial banking, defense systems, HIPAA healthcare systems.
B. Bridge Pattern (Shared Engine, Dedicated Schemas)
  • Architecture: All tenants share a single database server engine, but each tenant's data resides in its own isolated database schema (e.g. PostgreSQL schema_tenant123).
  • Advantages: Balances cost and isolation. Physical compute/RAM costs are shared, but logical database security boundaries are maintained by database engine permissions.
  • Disadvantages: Schema migration complexity; connection pool exhaustion if hundreds of schemas are active concurrently; shared server failure impacts all tenants.
  • Target Domain: Enterprise B2B SaaS platforms.
C. Pool Pattern (Shared Database, Shared Tables)
  • Architecture: All tenants share the same database instance, the same schema, and the exact same database tables. Every record contains a mandatory tenant_id discriminator column.
  • Advantages: Lowest cost, maximum server utilization, instantaneous onboarding of new tenants (zero schema creation needed), single migration run updates 100% of tenants.
  • Disadvantages: Highest security risk (a missing WHERE tenant_id = ? clause leaks data to competitors); requires strict Row-Level Security (RLS) enforcement; susceptible to the Noisy Neighbor effect.
  • Target Domain: High-volume consumer and SMB SaaS (Shopify, Slack, Notion).

Tenant Onboarding TimeMinutes to hours (DB provisioning)Seconds to minutes (Schema setup)Milliseconds (Single SQL INSERT)

Blast Radius on FailureIsolated to 1 tenantAll tenants on that DB engineAll tenants in that shared cluster
Noisy Neighbor VulnerabilityZero (Dedicated compute & RAM)Moderate (Shared IOPS/CPU)Severe (Shared table locks & memory)
Regulatory ComplianceMeets strict PCI-DSS / HIPAA rulesMeets moderate compliance rulesRequires complex audit controls

4. Row-Level Security (RLS) SQL Implementation

To prevent catastrophic cross-tenant data leaks in the Pool model, modern cloud applications utilize database-native Row-Level Security (RLS): 

-- 1. Enable RLS on multi-tenant table
ALTER TABLE customer_orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- 2. Create security policy checking current session tenant variable
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation_policy ON customer_orders
  FOR ALL
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant_id')::UUID);

-- 3. Application sets tenant context upon checkout connection
SET LOCAL app.current_tenant_id = 'a56f8901-b34e-4f12-98ab-3412567890ef';
-- Any subsequent SELECT * automatically filters only rows belonging to this tenant!
SELECT * FROM customer_orders; -- Impossible to see other tenant data even without explicit WHERE!

5. The Noisy Neighbor Problem & Mitigation Engineering

Problem: In a shared multi-tenant environment, if Tenant A runs an unindexed query scanning 10 million rows or executes a massive flash sale, it monopolizes CPU cores, RAM buffer pools, and database connection sockets, causing latency spikes and timeouts for innocent Tenant B on the same server.

Mitigation Strategies:

  • Token-Bucket Rate Limiting: Enforce strict per-tenant API rate limits (e.g. Tenant A is capped at 500 requests/sec with burst allowance of 1,000 via Redis token-bucket).
  • Database Connection Pool Segregation: Instead of a single shared pool, assign partitioned connection pools via PgBouncer so one tenant cannot starve available database sockets.
  • Linux Cgroups Quotas: Enforce hard CPU and memory ceilings per tenant container so runaway threads are throttled by the OS scheduler.
  • Automated Tenant Tiering ("Whale Migration"): Monitor real-time consumption. When a tenant outgrows the shared pool, automated workflows seamlessly migrate their database into a dedicated Silo instance without downtime.
[10 Marks] 4. Cloud Security Threats, Vulnerabilities & Forensics: Detailed Analysis of 4 Real-World Breaches (Capital One SSRF on IMDSv1, Microsoft Storm-0558 Token Forgery, Code Spaces Root Liquidation, Uber GitHub Leak) with Layered Defense-in-Depth Architecture. ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 2 Marks: Cloud attack surface, Shared Responsibility security boundaries, and OWASP Cloud Top 10 vectors.
  • 4 Marks: Comprehensive technical post-mortem of Capital One (SSRF/IMDSv1) and Microsoft Storm-0558 breaches.
  • 2 Marks: Forensic analysis of Code Spaces (Root account destruction) and Uber (Hardcoded API keys) incidents.
  • 2 Marks: Layered Cloud Defense-in-Depth blueprint across Perimeter, Network, IAM, Data, and Logging tiers.

1. The Cloud Attack Surface & Shared Responsibility

In cloud environments, traditional network perimeter defenses (firewalls, DMZs) are insufficient. Cloud workloads face unique vulnerabilities including metadata exfiltration, over-permissive IAM policies, container breakouts, and multi-tenant hypervisor escape. Under the Shared Responsibility Model, the cloud provider secures the underlying physical datacenters and virtualization hypervisors, but the enterprise customer is strictly responsible for identity management, access policies, operating system patching, and data encryption.

2. Case Study 1: Capital One SSRF Breach (2019) — AWS

  • The Vulnerability: A misconfigured open-source Web Application Firewall (ModSecurity WAF) deployed on an AWS EC2 instance was vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).
  • The Exploit Vector:
    1. The attacker sent crafted HTTP requests to the WAF, tricking it into executing internal network requests on behalf of the attacker.
    2. The WAF queried the internal AWS Instance Metadata Service v1 (IMDSv1) located at non-routable link-local IP http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/.
    3. IMDSv1 returned temporary AWS Security Token Service (STS) credentials assigned to the WAF's EC2 instance IAM role without requiring authentication.
    4. Due to a violation of the Principle of Least Privilege, the WAF IAM role had broad s3:* permissions across all S3 buckets in the AWS account.
    5. The attacker executed aws s3 sync and exfiltrated 106 million credit card applications and 140,000 Social Security Numbers from 700 S3 buckets.
  • Remediations & Architectural Lessons:
    • Migrate to IMDSv2: IMDSv2 is session-oriented. It requires a PUT request with a X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds header to obtain a session token before querying metadata, completely neutralizing SSRF attacks.
    • IAM Least Privilege: Instance profiles must only be granted access to the specific resources they need, never wildcard s3:*.
    • KMS Key Restriction: S3 buckets must be encrypted with Customer Managed Keys (CMK) containing key policies that restrict decryption exclusively to backend data pipelines.

3. Case Study 2: Microsoft Storm-0558 Token Forgery (2023) — Azure

  • The Vulnerability: An inactive Microsoft consumer account (MSA) cryptographic signing key leaked into a Windows kernel crash dump file following an internal system crash in April 2021. The dump was moved to an internet-connected debugging environment where threat actor Storm-0558 compromised it.
  • The Exploit Vector:
    1. The threat actors utilized the stolen private signing key to forge OpenID Connect (OIDC) bearer tokens.
    2. Due to a key validation issue in the Azure AD (Entra ID) token verification endpoint, the system erroneously accepted consumer-signed tokens for enterprise Microsoft Exchange Online and Outlook Web Access (OWA).
    3. The attackers accessed email inboxes of 25 major organizations, including the US State and Commerce Departments.
  • Remediations & Architectural Lessons:
    • Never allow cryptographic private keys to persist in plaintext memory crash dumps.
    • Enforce strict isolation between consumer identity verification endpoints and enterprise cloud endpoints.
    • Enforce automated Hardware Security Module (HSM) based key rotation with zero human access.

4. Case Study 3: Code Spaces Complete Liquidation (2014) — AWS

  • The Incident: Code Spaces was a SaaS provider offering code repositories and project management. Attackers gained access to their AWS Management Console root account.
  • The Exploit: The attackers demanded an extortion ransom. When Code Spaces attempted to regain control, the attackers systematically deleted all EBS volumes, S3 buckets, database snapshots, and off-site backup replicas.
  • The Impact: 100% of customer data and backups were permanently obliterated. Code Spaces was forced into immediate corporate liquidation within 12 hours.
  • Remediation: NEVER use the AWS root account for operational tasks. Enforce physical FIDO2 hardware MFA keys on root, lock root credentials in a corporate physical vault, and maintain cross-account immutable backups in an AWS Backup Vault with WORM compliance lock.

[10 Marks] 5. AWS IAM Enterprise Security Architecture: Identity Entities (Users, Groups, Roles), JSON Policy Grammar, 6-Step Evaluation Logic Algorithm with the Explicit Deny Rule, and Temporary STS Token Generation. ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 2 Marks: IAM foundational philosophy, Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP), and Zero Trust model.
  • 2 Marks: Detailed roles and differences of IAM Users, User Groups, IAM Roles, and IAM Policies.
  • 2 Marks: IAM JSON policy grammar, element definitions (Effect, Action, Resource, Condition), and complete JSON code example.
  • 3 Marks: Complete 6-step IAM Policy Evaluation Decision Flowchart and the absolute authority of Explicit Deny.
  • 1 Mark: AWS Security Token Service (STS) AssumeRole API temporary credential issuance.

1. Foundational IAM Security Principles

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the central control plane for security in Amazon Web Services. It governs authentication (who are you?) and authorization (what are you allowed to do?). IAM adheres to two mandatory security doctrines:

  • Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): Users, applications, and services must be granted only the absolute minimum permissions necessary to complete their job tasks, for the shortest duration required.
  • Zero Trust Architecture: Never trust, always verify. Every API request arriving at AWS endpoints is independently authenticated and authorized, regardless of whether it originates from inside or outside the VPC.

2. The Four Fundamental IAM Entities

  1. IAM Users: Persistent identity entities representing an individual person or service with long-term credentials (password for AWS Management Console, Access Key ID & Secret Access Key for CLI/SDK). Best practice: Avoid creating IAM users with static keys; prefer SSO federation.
  2. IAM User Groups: Collections of IAM users. Permissions assigned to a group automatically apply to all member users (e.g. DevelopersGroup, DBAdminGroup). Groups cannot be nested and cannot be identified as a Principal in a policy.
  3. IAM Roles: Temporary identities that can be assumed by anyone who needs it: human users, internal AWS services (e.g. an EC2 instance or Lambda function needing S3 access), or external federated identities via OIDC/SAML. Roles have NO long-term passwords or access keys; they issue short-lived temporary security credentials via AWS STS.
  4. IAM Policies: Formal JSON documents defining fine-grained permissions. Classified into Identity-based policies (attached to Users/Groups/Roles) and Resource-based policies (attached directly to AWS resources, such as S3 Bucket Policies or KMS Key Policies).

3. IAM JSON Policy Grammar & Syntax

Every IAM policy contains a mandatory structure defined by standard policy keys:

  • Version: Always specify "2012-10-17" (the current policy language version).
  • Statement: An array of individual permission rules.
  • Sid: Optional statement identifier for human documentation.
  • Effect: Required. Must be either "Allow" or "Deny".
  • Principal: Required in resource-based policies (indicates who is allowed/denied).
  • Action: Specific API calls permitted or forbidden (e.g. "s3:GetObject", "ec2:StartInstances").
  • Resource: Amazon Resource Name (ARN) identifying the target entity (e.g. "arn:aws:s3:::finance-reports/*").
  • Condition: Contextual constraints (IP address CIDR, MFA active, current time, SSL enforced).

Example: Production Least-Privilege IAM Policy with Explicit Deny & MFA Constraint:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AllowS3ReadWithMFA",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::gsfc-finance-vault",
        "arn:aws:s3:::gsfc-finance-vault/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true" }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ExplicitDenyOutsideCorporateNetwork",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "*",
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "NotIpAddress": {
          "aws:SourceIp": ["103.21.144.0/24", "115.112.45.10/32"]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

4. The 6-Step AWS Policy Evaluation Algorithm

When an authenticated principal issues an API request to AWS, the IAM Evaluation Engine processes all applicable policies through a strict deterministic algorithm:

  1. Step 1 (Default Implicit Deny): Every request begins in a state of default deny. Access is denied unless an evaluation step explicitly authorizes it.
  2. Step 2 (The Golden Rule — Explicit Deny Check): The engine evaluates all attached Identity-based policies, Resource-based policies, Service Control Policies (SCPs), Permissions Boundaries, and Session Policies. If ANY single policy statement contains an explicit "Effect": "Deny" matching the requested action and resource, the evaluation halts immediately and the request is REJECTED! Explicit Deny unconditionally overrides any number of Allows.
  3. Step 3 (AWS Organizations SCP Check): If AWS Organizations is active, Service Control Policies are evaluated. If an SCP denies access or does not allow it, access is denied.
  4. Step 4 (Resource-Based Policy Check): If a resource policy (e.g. S3 Bucket Policy) exists and contains an explicit Allow, the request is permitted (for same-account and cross-account requests).
  5. Step 5 (IAM Permissions Boundary & Identity Policy Check): If the principal has an attached Permissions Boundary, both the boundary AND the Identity Policy must allow the action.
  6. Step 6 (Final Determination): If at least one explicit Allow exists and zero explicit Denies exist, access is ALLOWED. Otherwise, it defaults back to DENY.

5. AWS Security Token Service (STS) & Temporary Credentials

When an EC2 instance, Lambda function, or federated engineer assumes an IAM Role, it calls the STS API:

aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/DeployerRole --role-session-name ProductionSession

STS returns three temporary credential components valid for a configurable duration (15 minutes to 12 hours):

  • AccessKeyId: Starting with prefix ASIA... (indicating temporary STS credentials, unlike long-term user keys starting with AKIA...).
  • SecretAccessKey: Ephemeral cryptographic secret.
  • SessionToken: Signed token string verifying credential authenticity with AWS endpoints.
[10 Marks] 6. Cloud Deployment Models & Enterprise Migration: Comprehensive Comparison of Public, Private, Hybrid (Cloud Bursting & Direct Connect), Community Clouds, Multi-Cloud Strategy, and the Gartner 6 R's Migration Framework. ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 3 Marks: Architectural definitions, characteristics, and use cases of Public, Private, Hybrid, and Community clouds.
  • 2 Marks: Hybrid Cloud Bursting mechanisms, dedicated interconnects (Direct Connect / ExpressRoute), and VPN tunnels.
  • 2 Marks: Modern Multi-Cloud strategy drivers (vendor lock-in avoidance, regulatory compliance, fault tolerance).
  • 2 Marks: Gartner 6 R's Cloud Migration Framework (Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Retain, Retire).
  • 1 Mark: 10-Parameter comparative evaluation matrix.

1. The Four Primary Cloud Deployment Models

  1. Public Cloud (e.g. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud):
    • Definition: Computing infrastructure owned and managed by a third-party cloud service provider, made available to multiple tenants over the public Internet.
    • Key Characteristics: Zero upfront CapEx, pay-as-you-go billing, infinite elastic scalability, multi-tenant resource sharing with logical virtualization isolation.
    • Ideal For: Startups, digital consumer applications, dynamic variable-workload web apps.
  2. Private Cloud (Internal / Corporate Cloud):
    • Definition: Cloud infrastructure provisioned for exclusive use by a single organization comprising multiple business units. Can be hosted on-premise (via OpenStack, VMware vSphere) or hosted by a third party.
    • Key Characteristics: Maximum data control, dedicated hardware (zero noisy neighbors), custom compliance governance, high initial Capital Expenditure (CapEx).
    • Ideal For: National defense agencies, central banks, proprietary intellectual property labs.
  3. Hybrid Cloud (Orchestrated Integration):
    • Definition: A composition of two or more distinct cloud infrastructures (private and public) bound together by standardized or proprietary technology that enables data and application portability.
    • Connectivity: Connected via high-throughput dedicated physical fiber lines (AWS Direct Connect / Azure ExpressRoute) backed up by encrypted IPsec VPN tunnels.
    • Cloud Bursting: An architectural pattern where mission-critical steady-state workloads run securely on the private cloud, but when demand exceeds 80% capacity during peak events, excess traffic dynamically "bursts" into the public cloud.
  4. Community Cloud:
    • Definition: Cloud infrastructure shared exclusively among several organizations having common missions, security requirements, regulatory compliance, or jurisdictional policies.
    • Example: Government agency clouds (US GovCloud), banking community networks (SWIFT cloud), medical research networks sharing genomic datasets.

2. Modern Enterprise Multi-Cloud Strategy

A Multi-Cloud Strategy involves utilizing services from two or more distinct public cloud service providers (e.g. AWS for general computing, GCP for BigQuery/TensorFlow AI, and Azure for Microsoft 365 / Active Directory).

  • Avoiding Vendor Lock-in: By containerizing applications with Docker and Kubernetes, enterprises avoid being held hostage to proprietary vendor pricing increases.
  • Data Sovereignty & Legal Compliance: Compliance with GDPR (Europe) and India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act requires citizen data to remain geographically inside national borders. Multi-cloud ensures datacenters exist in required jurisdictions.
  • Disaster Resiliency: If an entire cloud provider suffers a global outage (e.g. global AWS IAM or DNS failure), DNS traffic automatically routes to Azure.
