4. Gartner 6 R's Cloud Migration Framework

  1. Rehost ("Lift and Shift"): Migrating applications from on-premise servers directly to cloud VMs (EC2) without modifying code or architecture. Fastest migration with minimal risk, but fails to exploit cloud-native elasticity.
  2. Replatform ("Lift, Tinker and Shift"): Making targeted optimizations (e.g. migrating from on-premise self-hosted Oracle DB to AWS RDS managed database) without changing core application business logic.
  3. Refactor / Re-architect: Completely re-architecting the monolithic application into cloud-native microservices, serverless functions (AWS Lambda), and containerized Kubernetes clusters. Delivers maximum elasticity and lowest operational costs.
  4. Repurchase ("Drop and Shop"): Abandoning legacy in-house custom software in favor of a modern SaaS solution (e.g. migrating custom on-premise CRM to Salesforce, or legacy Exchange to Microsoft 365).
  5. Retain: Keeping applications on-premise that have strict low-latency hardware dependencies, recent capital investments, or regulatory constraints.
  6. Retire: Identifying redundant, obsolete, or underutilized applications during discovery and decommissioning them, saving 10% to 20% of enterprise IT budgets.
[10 Marks] 7. Enterprise Multi-Server 3-Tier Web Architecture: Layer Anatomy, Layer 4 (NLB) vs Layer 7 (ALB) Load Balancing, High Availability Math & SLA Downtime Calculations, and Disaster Recovery Strategies (RTO vs RPO). ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 3 Marks: Detailed VPC architectural diagram & component breakdown of Presentation, Application, and Persistence tiers.
  • 3 Marks: Technical comparison of Layer 4 (Transport / NLB) vs Layer 7 (Application / ALB) load balancing mechanisms.
  • 2 Marks: High Availability mathematical formulas (Serial vs Parallel Availability calculations) and SLA "Nines" table.
  • 2 Marks: Disaster recovery strategies (Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Region Active-Active) with RTO and RPO trade-offs.

1. Multi-Server 3-Tier Architectural Anatomy

Enterprise web applications decouple services into three independent layers to achieve fault isolation, independent scaling, and defense-in-depth:

  • Tier 1: Presentation / Web Tier (Public Subnet):
    • Directly accessible via Internet Gateway (IGW).
    • Fronted by an Internet-facing Application Load Balancer (ALB) terminating SSL/TLS 1.3 certificates.
    • Runs reverse proxies and static web servers (Nginx/Apache) serving cached React/HTML bundles. Zero business logic or database credentials exist in this tier.
  • Tier 2: Application / Logic Tier (Private Subnet):
    • Isolated from the public Internet; has no public IP addresses. Outbound internet updates occur via a NAT Gateway.
    • Runs backend APIs (Node.js, Spring Boot, Python) inside an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) that dynamically expands and contracts based on CPU or request queue metrics.
    • Utilizes an in-memory Redis / Memcached cluster to cache expensive database queries and session states.
  • Tier 3: Database / Persistence Tier (Isolated Subnet):
    • Completely locked down with zero inbound internet route. Accepts TCP traffic exclusively on port 3306/5432 originating from Tier 2 security groups.
    • Configured in a Multi-AZ High Availability topology: Primary Master instance in AZ-1 handles synchronous writes and replicates asynchronously to Standby Master in AZ-2 and Read-Replicas in AZ-3.

3. High Availability Mathematics & SLA Calculations

High Availability (HA) measures the percentage of time a system remains operational and accessible.

Fundamental Availability Formula:

Availability (A) = [ MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) ] × 100%

Where MTBF = Mean Time Between Failures, and MTTR = Mean Time To Repair.

System Composition Calculations:

  • Serial Components (Chain Dependency): If any component fails, the entire system fails. Overall availability is the product of individual availabilities:
    A_system = A_1 × A_2 × A_3
    Example: If Web Tier is 99% (0.99) and DB Tier is 99% (0.99), total availability is 0.99 × 0.99 = 98.01%!
  • Parallel Components (Redundancy): Redundant components running in parallel fail ONLY if both fail simultaneously:
    A_parallel = 1 - (1 - A_1) × (1 - A_2)
    Example: Two 99% redundant servers in parallel: 1 - (0.01 × 0.01) = 1 - 0.0001 = 99.99% (Four Nines)!
SLA LevelAvailability %Allowed Downtime per YearAllowed Downtime per Month
Two Nines99.0%3 days, 15 hours, 39 minutes7 hours, 18 minutes
Three Nines99.9%8 hours, 45 minutes, 57 seconds43 minutes, 49 seconds
Four Nines99.99%52 minutes, 35 seconds4 minutes, 23 seconds
Five Nines99.999%5 minutes, 15 seconds26 seconds

4. Disaster Recovery Strategies (RTO vs RPO Trade-offs)

Disaster recovery architectures are defined by two strict metrics:

  • Recovery Time Objective (RTO): The maximum acceptable duration of system downtime before service is restored.
  • Recovery Point Objective (RPO): The maximum acceptable duration of data loss measured in time (e.g. 1 hour of lost transactions).

[10 Marks] 8. Cloud Storage Architectures: Block Storage vs Object Storage vs File Storage, Distributed Consistency (CAP Theorem), and the Mathematics of 11-Nines (99.999999999%) S3 Durability. ▼
🎯 University Marking Scheme (10 Marks Blueprint):
  • 3 Marks: Architectural mechanisms, protocols, and data structures of Block Storage, Object Storage, and File Storage.
  • 2 Marks: 8-Parameter comparative matrix across all three storage paradigms.
  • 3 Marks: Mathematical explanation of 11-Nines (99.999999999%) durability and Erasure Coding (Reed-Solomon).
  • 2 Marks: Distributed Consistency, Eric Brewer's CAP Theorem, and S3 Lifecycle Automation tiers.

1. The Three Primary Cloud Storage Paradigms

  1. Block Storage (e.g. AWS Elastic Block Store - EBS, Azure Managed Disk):
    • Mechanism: Data is split into fixed-size raw blocks (e.g. 4 KB or 512 bytes), each identified by a unique sector address. The storage volume acts as a raw physical disk drive mounted over high-speed protocols (iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NVMe-oF).
    • Characteristics: Ultra-low sub-millisecond latency, high Input/Output Operations Per Second (IOPS), supports in-place random byte modifications.
    • Best Use Case: OS boot drives, ACID relational databases (Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL).
  2. Object Storage (e.g. AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob):
    • Mechanism: Data is stored as complete, self-contained, immutable binary objects in a flat namespace (buckets). Each object consists of three elements: Data Payload, Custom Metadata, and a globally unique Key (URI).
    • Access: Accessed exclusively over standard HTTP/HTTPS REST APIs using verbs: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD. No folders exist physically (delimiters like / are simulated prefix keys).
    • Characteristics: Massive petabyte/exabyte scalability, immutable (updates require complete replacement of the object), high latency compared to block storage, but virtually infinite concurrent read throughput.
    • Best Use Case: Media streaming, static website hosting, big data data lakes, long-term backups.
  3. File Storage (e.g. AWS Elastic File System - EFS, Azure Files):
    • Mechanism: Organizes data in a classic hierarchical folder-and-file directory tree adhering to POSIX filesystem standards. Mounted simultaneously across thousands of compute nodes via standard network protocols (NFSv4 for Linux, SMB/CIFS for Windows).
    • Characteristics: Supports concurrent multi-server read/write access, distributed file locking, automated elasticity.
    • Best Use Case: Shared web application assets (WordPress CMS), corporate shared network drives, distributed machine learning training datasets.

3. The Mathematics of 11-Nines (99.999999999%) S3 Durability

AWS S3 is engineered to provide 11 Nines (99.999999999%) of annual data durability.

What Does 11 Nines Mean Mathematically?

  • If an enterprise stores 10,000,000 (10 million) objects in AWS S3, statistically you can expect to lose a single object once every 10,000 years!
  • Annual probability of losing an object is $1 - 0.99999999999 = 0.00000000001 = 10^{-11}$.

Engineering Implementation:

  • Multi-AZ Geodistribution: S3 redundantly replicates data across at least three physically separated Availability Zones (AZs) located tens of kilometers apart within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and network backbones.
  • Erasure Coding (Reed-Solomon $k+m$): An object is partitioned into $k$ data fragments and $m$ parity fragments distributed across separate storage racks. Even if $m$ entire storage nodes or an entire datacenter completely burns down, the object is mathematically reconstructed from the remaining fragments in milliseconds with automated self-healing background daemons.

4. Distributed Consistency & Eric Brewer's CAP Theorem

Eric Brewer's CAP Theorem proves that a distributed storage system can guarantee at most two of the following three guarantees simultaneously:

  • Consistency (C): Every read receives the most recent write or an error.
  • Availability (A): Every non-failing node returns a successful response without timeout.
  • Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues operating despite arbitrary network dropped packets between nodes. Since network partitions are inevitable in physical cables, distributed cloud storage must ALWAYS select Partition Tolerance (P), forcing a trade-off between CP (HBase, MongoDB) or AP (Cassandra, CouchDB).
  • AWS S3 Strong Consistency: In December 2020, AWS upgraded S3 to deliver Strong Read-After-Write Consistency for all PUT, LIST, and DELETE operations with zero latency penalty and zero additional cost.

5. AWS S3 Storage Tiers & Automated Lifecycle Policies

  • S3 Standard: Frequent access; high throughput; 99.99% availability.
  • S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (IA): 50% cheaper storage; retrieval fee per GB.
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: Archive storage; retrieval in 1 minute to 5 hours.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Lowest cost ($0.00099/GB/month); retrieval in 12 to 48 hours; replaces magnetic tape vaults.
